chapters.title: Your first hour in Meridian
chapters.summary: Sign in, take the tour, find the ? menu, make search and shortcuts yours.

sections.text: Meridian reads your SAP data, tests it against fixed rules and lists every record that fails. Nothing here is a guess: each score, count and suggested value comes from a rule that ran over stored data. The first hour is about three things only: getting to the right starting page, learning the frame every page sits inside, and telling Meridian who you are.

sections.heading: Sign in and land where your work is
sections.text:
Accounts are created by an administrator. There is no self sign-up, so an invitation comes first. Open it, choose a password, then use your work email and that password to sign in.

Where you land depends on your role:

- Data stewards land on the fix list, with the worst records at the top.
- Data owners and approvers land on approvals, where fix batches wait for a second pair of eyes.
- Leads, analysts, SAP Basis and process analysts land on a home page for their role, which answers how healthy the data is and what to do next.

Your rights come from one main role plus any grants for a particular system or object. Pages and actions you have no part in are hidden rather than offered dead. If a colleague's home page looks different, use the view-as switch to read it: the layout changes, your permissions do not.

sections.heading: The frame around every page
sections.text:
Every page sits in the same frame. Four parts, and the product reads quickly once you know them.

- The index bar holds the pages you use daily, a **More** menu for the rest, search, the jobs tray, notifications, help and your user menu.
- The scope bar names where you are and carries two controls you will touch all day: a box that finds a failing record by key or name, and the run picker.
- The run picker decides which measurement every screen reads. The latest run follows the newest finished one. Pick an older run and Meridian keeps it as you move around, in this browser, until you set it back. Because the run sits in the page address, a link you copy shows a colleague exactly the same numbers.
- When your access covers one system or object only, a scope pill says which, so a figure is never mistaken for the whole landscape.

One warning worth taking early: you see the records your scope covers. If a colleague has records you cannot see, ask an administrator to check your grants.

sections.heading: Take the tour, then live in the ? menu
sections.text:
Open the help menu, marked **?**, on any page. Where a guided tour exists, it is offered there. Tours are short and shaped by role: one for stewards, one for leads, one for SAP Basis, one for processes. A tour jumps between pages for you and skips any step whose page has nothing to show yet. Take your role's tour now; every tour can be replayed later from [your preferences](/me/preferences).

The same menu holds the shortcuts sheet, what is new, this help centre with the user guide, and a report-a-problem dialog. Report a problem copies the page address, the current run and the version for you; opening it sends nothing anywhere.

sections.heading: Find things without hunting
sections.text:
Two boxes cover nearly everything.

- Press `?` to see which keys the page you are on answers to. Press `/` to jump into the record box, type two or more characters of a material number, a vendor name or a record key, then press Enter to open that record where it fails.
- Press Ctrl K, or `⌘K` on a Mac, to open search and jump. It lists every page your role can open. It also reads what you type with fixed rules rather than a model: an object name, a severity or dimension, a rule ID such as `MM003`, or a record key. Anything it cannot interpret opens the search page, which spans objects, rules, glossary terms, fix batches and runs.

Keys never fire while you are typing in a box, so both habits are safe to learn on the same morning.

sections.heading: Set your name, time zone and density
sections.text:
Your preferences sit at [Me, Preferences](/me/preferences) and are kept on the server, so they follow you to any browser.

Set your time zone first. Runs, schedules, due times and digests read sensibly once it is right; the default is UTC, which makes a 07:00 extraction look like an afternoon job. Then set locale, theme and row density, which retune rows, cards and spacing everywhere: compact suits a long fix list, comfortable suits a screen you share in a meeting.

Digests are off until you choose a cadence, so nothing arrives in your email until you ask for it. Where email is not configured on this deployment, notifications stay inside the product.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Connect a system, or check an existing one is healthy, at [Connect a system](/systems).
- Take a measurement with [Your first analysis run](/runs).
- Clean your first record in [Fix work](/fix).

chapters.title: Connect a system
chapters.summary: Add an SAP or cloud system, pass the connection test, let discovery and config load run.

sections.text: A system is one SAP source Meridian reads: an ECC instance, an S/4HANA landscape, a warehouse system, or a cloud product such as SuccessFactors, Ariba or Concur. Nothing else in Meridian works until at least one system is connected, tested and read. This chapter covers what you fill in, what a connection test actually checks, what happens after it passes, and where the secrets go.

sections.heading: What you name and what you choose
sections.text:
Give the system a name your team already uses, such as "PRD ECC", because that name appears on every run, score and report. Choose the type and the environment: production, quality or development. Types fall into two groups, and the group decides which fields you see.

- RFC types, which cover SAP ECC, S/4HANA on premise and Extended Warehouse Management: host, client, instance number, and a user with its password. The SAP user needs read authorisations only. Meridian never writes to SAP through this connection.
- Cloud types, which cover S/4HANA Cloud, BTP, SuccessFactors, Concur and Ariba: a base URL, an OAuth client ID and client secret, and a token URL where the product asks for one. SuccessFactors also accepts a plain user and password, signed in as the user at your company ID. Ariba asks for its realm and an application key beside the OAuth pair.

Leave a field you do not use empty rather than guessing a value. A guessed instance number or token URL shows up later as a failed job, not as a warning.

sections.heading: What a connection test checks
sections.text:
Test the connection before you save anything, and again after any change. The test signs in and then makes one short read as a probe, so it answers in seconds rather than waiting on a network stack that will not reply. A pass means both halves worked: the credentials are valid and Meridian can read at least one table through them.

When it fails, the message names the half that broke, and the place to look follows from it.

- A sign-in refusal means the user, password, client ID or client secret is wrong, or the secret has expired. Check the credentials on the connection settings.
- An unreachable message means the server could not get there at all. Check host and instance, then the route from the Meridian server: firewall rules, VPN, or an SAP router.
- A refused authorisation means sign-in worked but SAP will not let that user read one of the tables. Your Basis team grants read access to the tables and the RFC calls, then you test again.
- A timeout means the system answered too slowly to complete the probe. Test again at a quieter hour.
- A missing RFC library means the SAP connector is not installed on the worker. Ask an administrator to install it, or load that system's data from a file instead.

Meridian re-tests every connection every 30 minutes on its own, so a system that was healthy can show a problem before anyone looks. Treat degraded, unreachable and sign-in refused as work to do, not as noise.

sections.heading: What a good connection unlocks
sections.text:
Two steps follow a passing test, and they do different jobs.

Discovery of objects reads the system's structure: which tables exist, which fields they hold, which objects Meridian can extract at all. Until it runs, Meridian knows what it expects, not what you have. Discovery takes a while on a large landscape and shows its status on the system page; it is safe to leave and come back.

A configuration load reads the customising: which fields are required or suppressed, which values are valid, which parts of the product are switched on. That decides which rules apply. Until it loads, every rule applies by default, so an optional field in your configuration can read as a defect. A load can finish with gaps when some areas could not be read; rules that depend on those areas fall back to applying by default, and the page says how many areas loaded. Retry the gaps once the connection is healthy.

sections.heading: Where credentials live
sections.text:
Secrets are stored encrypted and scoped to your tenant, so another tenant's request cannot read them, and the page never shows a stored value back to you. They stay inside your own deployment: reading SAP data over this connection sends nothing outside it.

Because a secret belongs to the endpoint it was issued for, treat connection changes and secrets as one decision. Changing the host, the client, the base URL or the token URL means the old secret no longer matches the new target: retype it in the same edit, then test again. Leaving a secret field empty keeps the stored value, which is what you want when only the name or the description changed. Editing one field and keeping an old secret is a common cause of a sudden sign-in refusal.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Go to [Systems](/systems) to add a system, test it, and start discovery and a configuration load.
- Read what happens to the data next in [Your first analysis run](/runs).
- See which objects Meridian found for that system under [Objects](/objects).

chapters.title: Your first analysis run
chapters.summary: Extract, check, score — and read a run honestly, coverage flags included.

sections.text: An analysis run is one measurement of your data at one moment. Meridian reads the records, runs every applicable rule over them, and writes down what failed. Every score, failing record and suggested value you see afterwards belongs to that run. Make one now, while the steps are fresh, so the clean-up has something to compare with.

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.text:
A run has three parts, in this order.

1. Extraction reads the chosen objects from a system and stores the records, so the measurement can be repeated later without going back to SAP.
2. Checks apply each rule that applies to that system and configuration. A rule is one fixed test, so the same records give the same result every time.
3. Scoring turns pass rates into a data-quality score from 0 to 100: rules are grouped into six dimensions, the dimensions are weighted, and a critical failure can cap the total.

A run finishes when the analysis completes. Screens show finished runs only, so a run that is still going cannot mislead you with half numbers.

sections.heading: Choosing systems, objects and scope
sections.text:
Start from the system you connected. Choose the objects to read: material master, business partner, accounts payable, the warehouse objects. Pick one or two for a first run, so it finishes quickly and the result is easy to read.

Then set the scope. You can limit an extraction to company codes, plants, sales or purchasing organisations, and for transactional objects to a document date window. Leave a field empty to read everything it covers.

Scope matters more than people expect. A narrow scope gives an honest picture of the part of the landscape you chose and nothing else: the score is a figure for that scope, not a total for the installation. A wide first run may take hours and fill the fix list before anyone is ready to work it. One or two objects, a limited scope and a short period is the right first measurement.

sections.heading: Watching the job, then reading the overview
sections.text:
Open the jobs tray in the top bar to watch progress: each job shows its stage, how far it has got, and any error. A run is made of steps, and each step reports its own status and duration, so a failure says which part stopped.

Two things slow a first run more than anything else. An extraction that reads a whole table can run out of time; try a shorter period, or fewer objects at once. A large transactional object can exceed its memory budget, which is reported as a request to narrow the period. Neither is a fault in your data. Re-run with a smaller scope, and grow it once you know what each object costs. When the analysis finishes, the run builds its work list: the failing records, ranked worst first, ready for Fix work.

Read the run overview in this order, because the first number misleads on its own.

- The score and its cap. One critical rule failing over tolerance caps an object at 85, two or more at 70. The page names the rules that caused the cap, which is the shortest list worth fixing first.
- The findings, ranked by impact. Impact is failing records multiplied by a severity weight. It is a ranking, not a sum of money.
- The failing records behind a finding, with the field, the current value and, where Meridian has one, a suggested value.

sections.heading: Coverage badges, and what they mean
sections.text:
Sometimes a rule could not be evaluated, and a coverage badge says so. That is not a pass. A rule may be skipped because it does not apply to your loaded configuration, because the field it reads is not in the extract, or because the system cannot supply what the rule needs. A rule may also be suppressed until a date.

Read coverage before you compare scores. An object at 92 with forty applicable rules measured is a different claim from an object at 92 with six. Coverage names the basis: which rules were counted, over which records. Where coverage is thin, load the system's configuration and re-run, so unmeasured rules stop being invisible rather than being read as clean.

sections.heading: Comparing two runs
sections.text:
Comparison answers the question a first run cannot: is this better or worse than before?

Open Runs, tick two runs and compare them. Meridian shows which rules and records were fixed, which newly fail, and the score change. Only runs from the same source are comparable: extractions from one system form one lineage, and imported files are grouped by the objects they carry. Pin one run as the baseline to keep it as the reference; comparisons use the baseline when there is one and the previous run otherwise. You can rename a run so a steering pack refers to something a person recognises.

Two honest cautions. Rules that ran in only one of the two runs are left out of the change, so a new rule cannot read as a regression. And records a later run still finds failing return to the open list, which can make the open count rise in a good week.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Work the records the run found in [Fix work](/fix).
- Check the system behind the run at [Systems](/systems).
- Read the objects the run scored at [Objects](/objects).

chapters.title: Fix your first record
chapters.summary: One failing record, start to sign-off, and proof in the next run.

sections.text: A fix in Meridian is a decided value for one field of one record, a second person's approval, and a later run that proves the record now passes. Four steps, and the first takes two minutes. Do this once and the rest of the work list reads the same way.

sections.heading: Start from a finding
sections.text:
Open the fix list from a finding, or from Fix work directly. A finding is one rule that failed on records in one run, so arriving from a finding means the rule is already filtered: every record that failed it, worst first.

Pick the run in the scope bar first; the latest finished run is the default. If the list says no finished run exists, no analysis has completed. If it says the work list is not built, build it or choose a newer run. Filters worth using on day one: the object, the severity, and the switch for records with a suggested value. Those are the quickest way to learn the flow.

sections.heading: Read the record before you decide
sections.text:
The record panel gives you what you need, in a fixed order: the message that says what is wrong, the field and rule ID, the value the record holds now, and where a proposed value comes from.

The source matters. A suggestion can be the rule's own correction, tested by running the rule again on the new value; a fixed mapping from a known bad value to the right one; or a proposal from the cleaning engine, carrying a confidence. The first two have been checked against the rule. A cleaning proposal is a guess worth reading: check the value looks right for the record in front of you.

The panel also says why it matters, which is what goes wrong in SAP while the value stays as it is. Read that line once per rule, then trust it.

sections.heading: Accept a suggestion, type a value, or sign it off
sections.text:
Where there is a suggestion, accept it: one decision, and the record moves to a proposed state. Where there is none, enter the value yourself and save it. If what you type still fails the rule, Meridian says so before it goes anywhere. A record with several issues can have several suggestions; accept them together rather than one by one.

Keys, once you are working a list: `j` and `k` move, `a` accepts the suggestions on the record you are on, `t` takes it so colleagues see it is yours, `u` undoes a decision, `Enter` opens the full record. After each decision the next record comes up by itself, which is the point: you are working a queue, not browsing.

Sometimes the data is right and the rule is wrong for it: a legacy material that will never be ordered again, a vendor legitimately missing a tax number. Mark it not an issue and write the reason. That reason is not a formality: it is the record of a decision, it sits in the history and the audit log, and the second person reads it when they review your batch. Where the value is genuinely wrong but the business will correct it later, accept the risk instead: the same sign-off, a different meaning. Both need the right to sign records off, and both can be withdrawn, which returns the record to the open list.

sections.heading: What a draft batch is
sections.text:
Every value you accept or type goes into your own draft batch. It is private work in progress: it touches nothing, and nobody waits for it. A batch is a set of corrections approved and exported together, and it stays a draft until a second person approves it.

The four-eyes rule has no bypass. Whoever drafted a batch cannot approve or export it, which is why a steward's batch is opened by a data owner or another steward.

When you hand over, say what is in it. Forty accepted values against one mapping rule is easy to approve. A batch mixing three objects, a dozen rules and six sign-offs is not, and it will come back to you.

sections.heading: From sign-off to SAP, and proof
sections.text:
An approver reads the diff and approves. The batch then waits to be exported as a file for your SAP load process, in whichever format your team uses. Meridian never changes SAP on its own: live write-back is a separate route, off unless an administrator enabled it, and each request needs someone other than the requester. Records then read sent to SAP, and nothing is confirmed yet.

Confirmation comes from a run. The next finished run of that system reads those records again. A record that now passes becomes fixed and leaves the open list. A record that still fails returns to it, with a warning that the value was sent and did not take.

When that happens, in order: check the exported file was loaded completely and into the right client; check the run you are viewing finished after the load, because only later runs reconcile; then check whether SAP wrote the value back itself, or the record now fails a different rule. Enter another value if you need to, and it goes through approval again.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Work the queue in [Fix work](/fix).
- See what waits for you, and who it waits on, at [Inbox](/inbox).

chapters.title: A day as a data steward
chapters.summary: Prioritise by value, work whole rule sets, keep the queue honest.

sections.text: Steward work is a queue, not a hunt. The records that need you are already listed, ranked and filtered by what the last run found. The skill is choosing the order, and keeping the numbers honest so your owner can plan around them.

sections.heading: Rank the day by severity-weighted value
sections.text:
The fix list is worst first, and worst means severity-weighted: a rule's failing records multiplied by its severity, critical counting highest. That ranking is a decent first guess, but two adjustments make a real plan.

Critical records first, always. A critical failure blocks SAP processes and caps the object's score, so the cap does not lift until they are cleared. Work the critical count down before anything else in an object.

Then look at what you can clear in bulk. One rule failing on 8,000 records with the same checked suggestion is a morning. Ten records each needing a different typed value is also a morning, and moves the score by nothing. Severity-weighted value is the ranking; volume times a checked suggestion is the shortcut.

sections.heading: Work a whole rule across an object
sections.text:
Open the object and work its issues from the list on the left rather than scrolling a flat record list. That list groups everything by rule, worst first, with how many records are open and how many have a suggestion. Pick one rule and drive it to zero.

This beats record order for three reasons. You learn one rule's logic and apply it 500 times, so each decision gets quicker. You can set one value across every open record of that rule, the single most productive action in the product. And the object's score moves in one step, so your owner sees progress today rather than in three weeks.

Set-one-value deserves care. It is offered on blank fields by default, so filled values are left alone. Read the count it covers, and check a handful of records first to confirm the rule's problem really is the same problem in all of them.

sections.heading: Bulk accepts, and proposals worth trusting
sections.text:
You can select records and accept their suggestions together, take them, or mark them not an issue with one reason. At very large counts this is intended behaviour.

It stops being safe when you cannot say what the value is. Accepting a suggestion that was re-tested against its own rule is a different act from accepting a low-confidence cleaning proposal. On the second kind, read a sample: ten records. If the proposed value is wrong in a third of them, stop and send the rule back to whoever maintains it rather than approving 3,000 guesses into a batch.

The proposals tab holds values the cleaning engine suggests, grouped by object and field with their confidence. Review a group, accept or reject each, then draft a fix batch from what you approved. Rejecting is useful and remembered: a rejected value or pair is recorded so it is not proposed the same way again. Reject the same kind of suggestion every week and the rule needs tuning, not you. Say so with the rule ID: a rule whose false-positive rate stays high is visible to whoever owns rules.

Bulk sign-offs carry the same warning in reverse. Marking a thousand records not an issue with one reason is a policy decision, not stewardship, and it needs the approve permission precisely because it should be somebody's deliberate call.

sections.heading: Keep the queue honest
sections.text:
Take the records you are actually working, and release the ones you are not. Assignment exists so colleagues and your owner can see what is held. A record taken three weeks ago and untouched reads as work in progress that is not happening.

Three habits keep the numbers true. Set the queue to yours and clear your own overdue items before picking up new ones. Empty your draft batch: accepted values sitting undrafted stay open forever, and open work is not fixed work. And when a run shows a value you sent did not take, reopen it rather than accepting it again into a new batch, because the load is usually the reason.

Your owner sees open work per person, critical and overdue counts, and the decisions you have made: accepted suggestions, typed values, sign-offs, approvals. Read that as a workload signal, not a scoreboard. Use it to make sure the view shows what you are really holding.

sections.heading: Recurrence, and what owners see
sections.text:
Some fixes come back. A record was fixed, a later run finds it failing again, and it returns to your list. A rule with a high recurrence rate is telling you the cause is upstream: a process, an interface or a default in SAP keeps writing the bad value, and no amount of cleaning will hold.

Spot it early. When the same record key fails the same rule after two loads, stop cleaning it. Write what you found in the record's note, name the rule to your owner, and let the fix go to configuration or to the interface. That is worth more to the programme than a third clean of the same vendor.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Get a batch through review in [Reviewing and approving fix batches](/inbox?kind=approvals).
- See what your owner sees about backlog at [Owners](/insights/owners).
- Work duplicates and golden records in [Master data](/mdm).

chapters.title: Reviewing and approving fix batches
chapters.summary: Read the diff, approve or send back, and know what write-back does.

sections.text: You are the second pair of eyes. Every value that reaches SAP has been decided by one person and approved by another, and you are usually the other. The rule is absolute: whoever drafted a batch cannot approve or export it. Your job is not to re-do the steward's work but to decide whether it is safe to load.

sections.heading: What lands in Approvals
sections.text:
Open the approvals list in the inbox. Two kinds of thing wait there.

Fix batches are the main one. Each row names the rules it fixes, who requested it, how many records it holds, and its first change, written as the SAP field, the record and the pair of values: the old one, then the new one. Filters separate what is waiting for approval from what is approved, exported, or everything.

SAP write-back requests are the other kind. They ask Meridian to send an approved change straight into SAP rather than through a file. Live write-back is off unless an administrator turned it on; where it is off, the card says so and fixes go out as files. You cannot approve a request you made, any more than your own batch.

Merge decisions and other master-data approvals arrive here too, but the daily load is batches.

sections.heading: Read the diff before you approve
sections.text:
Open the batch and read it as a change set, not as a count. Four things answer most questions.

- Items: every record with its field, the value it holds now, the value proposed, where the proposal came from, and its confidence. Values from a rule that has been re-tested against the rule are strong; cleaning engine proposals with low confidence deserve a look at the actual record.
- Before and after: each changed field as `TABLE.FIELD` with old and new values. This is the line you are actually approving.
- Who and when: the drafter, the history of the batch, and every change made to it.
- Exported files, once it has been exported: format, who exported, who approved, and the file's fingerprint, so you can check that the file loaded into SAP is the file Meridian produced.

Check the shape of the batch too. A batch of one rule and one object with a consistent change is easy to reason about. A batch spanning several objects, mixing typed values and sign-offs, is worth sending back for splitting even if every individual value looks fine.

sections.heading: Approving, and sending back
sections.text:
Approve when the changes are right, or when they are right enough to load and the rest can be fixed afterwards. Say what you approved and when, which the batch records for you.

Send back when one of these is true. The reason on a sign-off does not hold, or is missing. The values look accepted in bulk without being read. The batch includes records you cannot see the effect of. The proposed value fails a rule you can name. Sending back is not a verdict on the steward; it is the control working. Put the reason in words the drafter can act on, and reference the rule ID.

While a batch is still a draft you can change a proposed value yourself: pick the item, type the correct value, and that is what goes forward. Do it for one obvious correction rather than bouncing a whole batch for one field.

Withdrawing a sign-off is a separate act from approving a batch, and it needs the same right that made the sign-off. If a record was marked not an issue and you disagree, withdraw it: the record returns to the open list with the withdrawal recorded, and the steward sees why. Use it for a decision that was wrong, not for a decision you would merely have made differently.

sections.heading: When the change reaches SAP
sections.text:
Approval does not touch SAP. It is Meridian's record that the values are correct. The approved batch is then exported as a load file, in whichever format your team's process uses, and your own controlled process loads it: Migration Cockpit, a mass change, or a mass maintenance run.

Where live write-back is switched on and approved, the change goes to SAP through that route instead. Either way, the record's status moves to sent to SAP, and the work is not finished until a run says so.

The next finished run of that system reconciles every exported record. Those that pass become fixed. Those that still fail return to the fix list, and the batch shows them as still failing after export. That figure is yours to watch: a batch with a high still-failing count points at the load, the client, or a rule that keeps losing to an interface.

sections.heading: What to ask before you say yes
sections.text:
Short questions, quickly answered from the batch itself.

- Who drafted this, and have I approved their work before?
- What changed in SAP between the run the batch was cut from and now?
- Is any of this a critical value that blocks a process, where an unnecessary change costs more than leaving it open?
- Does the reason on each sign-off explain why the business accepts it?
- Can I say what one wrong value in here would cost? If not, look at the records that hold keys used by other objects.
- Has the same rule been approved and re-fixed twice? Then approve this load and raise the rule, not the steward.
- Would I be comfortable if an auditor read this batch, this reason and this name beside my approval? That is exactly what they will do.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- See the work the batch came from in [Fix work](/fix).
- Check which rules are failing most at [Failing rules](/insights/rules).
- Read the full approval reference in [the user guide](/docs).

chapters.title: Keeping the plumbing healthy
chapters.summary: Schedules, extraction and discovery runs, memory guards, jobs and retries.

sections.text: Basis work in Meridian is the supply chain: connections that still work, extracts that land on time, configuration that matches SAP, and jobs that either finish or say why they did not. Do it well and everyone downstream sees current numbers without asking. Do it late and every score on every page quietly goes stale.

sections.heading: Schedule the extracts
sections.text:
Data changes in SAP every day, so a run is a photograph, not a feed. Scheduled re-evaluation keeps the photograph recent: choose an object, a schedule and a mode, and add it. An extraction reads the tables behind the objects you selected, filtered by the scope you set, and stores them as a run; nothing is written back, because the connection is read-only. The analysis then applies the rules that apply to that system and builds the work list. If you run an extract alone, the analysis is a second step over the same stored data, which is the cheap way to test a rule change.

Two modes cover nearly everything. A full download reads every record of the object. Changes only re-reads the records SAP's change log shows as changed, which is quicker and lighter, at the cost of trusting the log; Meridian takes a full download at least weekly so a gap in the log cannot hide.

Choose the schedule from the work downstream, not from the calendar. A weekly clean-up needs a run before stewards start, not after. Approvals and exports land on a Wednesday, so the confirming run should be Thursday. Daily deltas on the objects people actually fix, and a weekly full on everything else, is a sane default.

sections.heading: Memory guards and time limits
sections.text:
Large transactional objects can outgrow the budget of a single job. When they do, the job stops with a memory message that asks you to narrow the period, and that is exactly the right instruction: shorten the document date window, split the object across runs, or move it to changes only.

Read these as sizing feedback, not data faults. The same scope will keep failing at the same size. If an object is genuinely that big, narrow the period permanently, schedule it that way, and say so on the object page so nobody re-widens it. A timeout at a busy hour is a different signal: retry the step quietly before you change anything.

sections.heading: Process discovery runs
sections.text:
Discovery reads the document and change tables of a business process and reconstructs how it actually ran: which steps, in what order, by whom, on how many cases. It is heavier than an ordinary extract and takes from a few minutes to a couple of hours depending on volume, so plan it rather than clicking it during a meeting.

Three things catch people. A process needs enough cases to mean anything, so a rarely used path gives a thin model rather than a wrong one. Only one discovery chain runs against a system at a time, and a chain that waits too long reports that extraction on the system was still running. And the licence may not include the modules a process's event log reads: such a process is marked as not in this licence, cannot be selected, and no amount of retrying changes that. Ask whoever holds the licence what is entitled before you plan around a process.

Once a run finishes, the process page shows coverage, fitness, variants and duration, and the data-quality defects on the objects that process touches.

sections.heading: Config loads
sections.text:
A configuration load reads the customising: which fields are required or optional, which values are valid, which parts of the product are switched on. That is how Meridian decides which rules apply. Without it, every rule applies by default, and a field your configuration never uses reads as a defect on every record.

Load the configuration on a new system before anyone reads a score from it. Re-load after a configuration change in SAP, and after any upgrade that touches the tables you monitor, so a change in score can be traced to a change in SAP rather than to the data. A load can finish with gaps when some areas could not be read; the rules that depend on those areas fall back to applying by default, and the page tells you how many areas loaded. Retry the gaps once the connection is healthy, and treat a persistent gap as a missing authorisation rather than a bug.

sections.heading: Jobs, retries and alerts
sections.text:
The jobs tray shows what is running now. The jobs list shows extractions, analyses, uploads and simulations with their status, duration and any error, and a failed run breaks into steps, each with its own message.

When a job fails, read the sentence rather than the stack. A sign-in refusal means credentials. An unreachable message means host, port or network route. A refused authorisation means the connection user cannot read one of the tables, which is a request to your SAP team. A missing library means the SAP connector is not installed on the worker. Fix the cause, then retry the failed step or re-run the analysis: retrying without fixing just refills the list. A run that stays running for a long time usually means the background workers have stopped, which is an infrastructure check, not a data one.

Alert channels carry the news out: email, Slack, Teams or a webhook, each with a digest and a test you can send. Alerts carry counts, rule IDs and links, never record values, which is what makes them safe to leave on a shared channel. Send a test when you add one, and point a channel at the two events worth waking someone for: a system that stopped being reachable, and a run that failed before it scored.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Manage connections, loads and schedules at [Systems](/systems).
- Review discovery runs and process models at [Processes](/process).
- Set channels, retention and health checks at [Settings](/admin/settings).

chapters.title: Reading the insights
chapters.summary: Rules, trend, forecast, root causes, duplicates — and what a 100 does not say.

sections.text: Insights answer what a fix list cannot: which problems matter most, whether the clean-up is working, and what a number refuses to tell you. Every view reads the run in the scope bar, so check which run you are on before you repeat a figure.

sections.heading: Failing rules: what breaks most
sections.text:
The rules view ranks rules by impact: failing records multiplied by a severity weight, critical counting highest. It is a ranking of where to put people, not money.

Read three things before you act. The pass rate says how much of what the rule checked failed, and is honest only with its basis: a rule that checked nine records tells you less than one that checked nine hundred. The change since the last run of the same system says whether it is growing or shrinking; only rules that ran in both runs are compared, so a rule you switched off cannot read as a fix. The object and field say who has to be involved to change it.

Open a rule and you get the finding: what failed, how many records, why it matters, samples, and the fix. That is the normal route into clean-up work. A few rules account for most of the impact, so work that handful first.

sections.heading: Progress and trends: did the fix stick
sections.text:
A trend answers a narrower question than a score does. It re-scores a system's finished runs under today's weights, so the comparison is like for like, and never crosses lineages.

Did a fix stick is a different test from did a fix happen. A value you approved is not a fix. A record a later run found passing is. Check three things in order: the open count falling, the fixed count rising in a later run, and the recurrence figure, which counts issues that failed again after being fixed.

A high recurrence rate on one rule is the most useful signal in the view. It says the cause is upstream: an interface, a default or a setting keeps writing the bad value, and cleaning those records again moves the numbers and changes nothing on the ground. Where the pace is flat there is no projected finish, and the page says so rather than inventing one.

sections.heading: Forecast, and its limits
sections.text:
The forecast projects each object's score 7, 30 and 90 days ahead, and needs finished runs on three different days before it will draw a line. The shaded band is the range the score is likely to fall in: read the band, not the tip of the line.

The assumption in the name is the method. It continues the recent trend, which means the same objects are worked, at the same pace, under the same rules, and nothing new breaks. That makes it useful as a warning and poor as a plan: it cannot know about a mass change you are about to load, or a rule you are about to publish.

Say its limits wherever the figure appears. It is per object, so there is no single forecast for the landscape, and a thin history gives a smooth line rather than a reliable one. An object held down by a cap can jump the moment one rule clears, which a line drawn from small changes will not predict.

sections.heading: Root causes and duplicates
sections.text:
The root causes view groups failures by origin rather than by record. It separates a data problem, a value that is simply wrong or missing, from a configuration problem, where the field or setting means the rule cannot be satisfied as things stand. The distinction decides who does the work: data goes to stewards, configuration to whoever owns customising. Cleaning records against a configuration problem wastes the week, because the next record is wrong the same way.

Duplicates come from match rules, which compare one field at a time and score each pair a confidence. The [duplicates](/insights/duplicates) view shows a cluster of records that appear to describe the same thing. Pick the record that should survive and create a merge proposal, which is a request, not an action: a second person compares the pair, gives a reason, and merges or rejects it. Do not merge in bulk. A wrong merge is worse than a duplicate, because it ends one record's history quietly.

sections.heading: Coverage honesty
sections.text:
A high score says the rules that ran, on the records they checked, mostly passed. It does not say the data is good.

Before you quote a score, check the basis. How many rules apply to that object, and how many have ever run? If no configuration was loaded, rules apply by default and measure the wrong thing. If an imported file had no column for a required field, every check that needed it was skipped. If a rule is suppressed until a date, its failures are out of the score for now. Where a rule could not be evaluated, a coverage badge says so, and that is not a pass.

Ask three questions of any score you report: how many rules, over how many records, how many skipped. A 100 built on four rules over a narrow scope is not a clean object. It is an unmeasured one.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Rank the work at [Failing rules](/insights/rules).
- Check whether the backlog is falling at [Progress](/insights/progress).
- Read the projection, and its limits, at [Forecast](/insights/forecast).

chapters.title: Reporting up
chapters.summary: Exec view, board pack, owner digests, scheduled reports, measured money.

sections.text: Reporting in Meridian is choosing the honest number that answers the question, and saying what it does not cover. The pages already hold the figures; the work is framing them for people who decide things with them.

sections.heading: The executive view and the board pack
sections.text:
The executive view is one page for leadership: the score and what caps it, readiness by wave, value at risk, and owners. Its first line is the verdict, so a reader who stops after thirty seconds has the accurate impression rather than the comfortable one.

The board pack is the shareable form of the same page, carrying the same deltas as the screen: what changed against the run before it, in the same lineage. A pack with no earlier run says nothing changed, which is a fact about your history rather than the data, and worth writing into the covering email yourself.

Presentation mode drops the navigation so any insight page fills a room's screen. Use it rather than screenshots: the run the figures come from is named on the page. Quote a score with its run, its date and its basis, which is the rules counted and the records they ran over. A percentage without its basis is not evidence.

sections.heading: Owner scorecards and digests
sections.text:
The owners view shows score and open work per owner, lowest score first, each with the digest that owner receives. It answers who has to act, not which object is prettiest.

Send a digest from there, to one owner or to everyone with open items, and the same text arrives as a notification now; the standing schedule is unchanged.

A scorecard is only fair if ownership is real, so start with the [objects](/objects) list, where each object names an owner and a steward. Unassigned work shows as nobody yet, and it does not move: a third of a backlog with no name is a staffing finding, not a data finding. Keep assignments current when people change roles.

sections.heading: Schedules, and the audit trail
sections.text:
A schedule generates a report on a cadence and delivers it to named users as a notification and an email attachment, or to configured channels. Email channels get the file; chat channels and webhooks get a link to the report library, because they carry no files. Recipients need the export right, or they are not sent it.

Set the schedule's time zone to the zone the readers live in. A Monday pack that lands at 02:00 local time is read late or not at all, and slots are computed in the zone you enter. A slot missed while the server was down is not back-filled, so check the schedule's history before treating a missing report as a data problem. Scheduled generation also needs the report export feature in your licence: where it is missing, a slot is skipped rather than sent, so confirm a new schedule by hand.

Auditors want evidence of control, not a score. Export the audit log for the period: it records every decision, approval and export with who, when and against which record, and an export holds a bounded number of rows, so narrow it by date. Fix batches read as four-eyes evidence, drafter and approver both named and timed, and exported files carry a fingerprint, so the file loaded can be matched to the file Meridian produced. The audit proves who decided, not that the value was right.

sections.heading: Comparing runs for steering material
sections.text:
Steering committees ask whether the programme is on track, which is a comparison, not a snapshot. Pin a baseline run, usually the run after a clean-up or at programme start, and later comparisons read against it.

Tick two runs to compare them: which rules and records were fixed, which newly fail, and what each object's score did. Only rules that ran in both runs are compared, so a rule switched off cannot flatter the trend. Export the result as a proof of progress report or a comparison workbook, and put record counts beside the score: a rise built on a smaller extract will not survive a sceptical question. Where the pace is flat there is no projected finish and the page says so; report that honestly, since it is a better steering item than an invented date.

sections.heading: Proven cost, and value at risk
sections.text:
These two money figures mean different things and must never be merged into one headline.

Proven cost is measured. It is money already posted in SAP on documents with a defective value, such as a payment sent twice. It happened, it is in the ledger, and it is reported per top-level process in your configured currency, never added across processes, because one record can sit in more than one flow.

Value at risk is priced, not measured. It is affected records multiplied by the value per record your tenant set for that feature, in its cost model. A feature nobody priced shows no value, so a blank is a configuration gap rather than a zero. Quote it with its formula, never as a saving.

In one line: proven cost is money you have already lost, value at risk is money you have agreed is exposed. Neither invites a third figure the tool did not compute.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Open the one-page leadership view at [Executive summary](/insights/exec).
- Check scores and open work per owner at [Owners](/insights/owners).
- Set schedules and download the pack at [Reports](/insights/reports).

chapters.title: Rules: tune, author, learn
chapters.summary: Suppressions, dry-runs, natural-language drafts, learned rules, why proofs exist.

sections.text: Rules are the fixed tests your scores are built from. When a score looks wrong, the cause is usually a rule that is wrong for your configuration rather than data that is wrong for the business. Tuning is normal work: a rule pack ships wide, and your job is to narrow it to what is true here.

sections.heading: Read a rule before you judge it
sections.text:
Open a rule to see its last pass rate, its description, the fields and tables it reads, its severity, dimension and grain, its owner and its versions. The message and instruction you meet in a record panel come from this page, so if stewards cannot tell what to do with a finding, the fix belongs here.

Check three things when a rule seems wrong. Its basis: which records it actually ran over. Its applicability: whether the field is required, optional, suppressed or absent in your configuration. Its grain: one purchase order with five bad lines is one failing document and five failing lines, and the pass rate means different things at each.

sections.heading: Disable, or suppress with an expiry
sections.text:
A rule that flags a field your configuration never uses is not strict, it is wrong. Switch it off, or open it and disable it. The change takes effect from the next run; past runs keep their results, so an old report does not quietly alter itself. Do this in the open: say which rule, on which system, and why. A disabled rule nobody can explain is how an audit finding appears two years later.

Suppressions are the softer tool and the one to try first. A suppression keeps a rule, or a single record, out of the score until a date, with the reason and who made it. Use one when the rule is right but the fix is scheduled: a bank key a migration will correct in November, a plant that closes next quarter. The date matters. Set it for when the fix lands, not for a comfortable review cycle, and look at the list when suppressions expire. A rule suppressed twice in a row is a rule your configuration does not support, and it should be rewritten or disabled rather than suppressed a third time.

The two are not the same decision. Disabling changes what the rule pack asserts about your landscape. Suppressing defers a known defect, with an owner and a date. Suppression needs the approve permission, and it should need a name too.

sections.heading: Dry-run before you publish
sections.text:
Never publish a rule on the strength of how it reads. Choose a finished run and dry-run against it: Meridian applies the draft to the stored records and reports how many it checked, how many failed, and samples of the failures with values masked. The rule becomes active only after a clean dry run, and applies from the next run onwards.

The honest test is a dry run against your latest data, for a blunt reason: the newest run holds the records you would actually flag tomorrow. A dry run against an old run measures defects that may already be cleaned, so a rule that fails nothing there may fail nine thousand records now. If a rule's failure count changes more than threefold between two recent runs of the same scope, ask which run is the exception before you trust either.

Expect a first dry run to over-report. That is the point: the number tells you which condition to add, not whether the idea is sound. Publishing and writing need the manage-rules permission, and the author of a rule version cannot approve it.

sections.heading: Drafts in words, and rules learned from your data
sections.text:
Where drafts are held, you can describe a check in ordinary language and generate a draft rule. The model sees field metadata and aggregate statistics: table and field names, data dictionary attributes, counts, lengths, formats. It never sees a record value, and what it produces is a draft, labelled as generated, that you review, dry-run and publish yourself. Treat it as a first attempt by a junior analyst who knows the schema and nothing about your business: usually structurally right, occasionally asserting something your configuration does not do.

Meridian can also read your own data for regularities it did not assume. A learned rule is a pattern your records follow consistently, such as a field effectively decided by another field, or a value combination nobody uses. Each comes with its support: how much of the data follows it. Approve one and it becomes an active rule at medium severity; reject it and it is gone.

A pattern at very high support is a house convention worth checking against the business. Sometimes it is the real rule. Sometimes it is a defect everyone has learned to live with, which is exactly the case where a new rule makes noise and a configuration change is the answer. Check the records it would fail before you approve, and re-check after the next run rather than assuming it landed well.

sections.heading: Proofs: a rule must fail something
sections.text:
Every shipped rule carries a proof: a record that makes it fail, and a record that makes it pass. Conditional rules carry both branches, one where the condition holds and one where the rule is skipped.

The reason is uncomfortable but sound. A rule that has never failed anything is not evidence of clean data; it is evidence the rule cannot see the data. Requiring each rule to fail something and pass something catches the three mistakes that make a rule pack quietly useless: a field name that does not exist, a condition that never matches, and a check that fires on every record and gets switched off within a week.

When you review a rule of your own, ask the same two questions before publishing: what record does this catch, and what record does this let through? If a dry run cannot answer both, the rule is not ready.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Tune what applies at [Rules](/rules).
- Write and dry-run a draft at [Rule drafts](/rules/drafts).
- Review patterns from your own data at [Learned rules](/rules/learned).

chapters.title: Master data: survivors and golden records
chapters.summary: Survivorship, match rules, merge review, the glossary as shared language.

sections.text:
Master data work answers one question: when the same supplier, customer or material exists in more than one place, which record is the one people trust? Meridian finds the pairs, proposes the values, and asks a person to decide. The output is a golden record: one best version of an entity, with a link back to every source it was built from.

Stewards review matches and merges. Analysts check coverage and health. Administrators set the rules that decide. Everyone reads the same pages, and nothing here is automatic without a person in the loop.

sections.heading: What survivorship decides
sections.text:
When sources disagree, survivorship chooses the value the golden record keeps, one field at a time. A telephone number from the newest record, a payment term from a trusted system, an address from whichever source actually fills it: a field's rule can be the most recent, the most complete, a chosen system, or the most frequent value.

Two facts avoid most surprises. Until a field has a rule, the most recent source value wins, which is a default rather than a decision. And every rule shows whether a person set it or it was suggested from the data; a suggested rule does nothing until a person activates it.

Read the field list before you activate anything. The fields that matter are the ones downstream processes key on: name, address, bank details, payment terms, tax classification. A rule on a note field is not worth review time. A rule you did not set on a payment term will decide money.

sections.heading: Match rules at a glance
sections.text:
[Match rules](/mdm/match-rules) decide what counts as the same thing. Each rule compares one field, exactly or fuzzily, phonetically for names, by numeric range for amounts, or semantically, and carries a weight and a threshold; the pair scores a confidence between 0 and 1.

The three bands are what you tune. Pairs at or above the auto-merge point merge on their own. Pairs between the review floor and that point go to a steward. Pairs below the floor are left alone. Raising the floor sends fewer pairs to people and hides real duplicates; lowering it buries stewards in obvious non-matches. The honest setting is the one where a steward agrees with most of what reaches them.

Two tools make this safe. A simulation shows the candidate pairs a rule would produce and how they split across the three bands. A tuning dry run re-scores the newest stored pairs with the weights and thresholds you enter, and saves nothing. Constraints are the pairs pinned as do not match or always match, created when a steward decides, and they stop the same wrong pair coming back.

Editing rules needs the manage-rules permission. Coverage matters more than cleverness: an object with no match rule has no duplicates found, which looks identical to having none.

sections.heading: Reviewing a merge
sections.text:
Every candidate pair is decided in [match review](/mdm/golden/merge), where the two records sit side by side, differing fields highlighted and identical ones folded away. You give a reason, then merge, mark it not a match, or skip; the next pair opens by itself. On the keyboard, `j` and `k` move, `m` merges, `n` marks not a match and `s` skips, and a decision needs a reason before it goes in.

Merging needs the approve permission, and it is the least reversible act in this part of the product. Read the two records as a person who has to explain the merge later: write "same vendor, one entered with the suffix and one without", not "duplicate".

What a merge does is concrete. The surviving record keeps its values, blank fields are filled from the other, and the other is marked superseded rather than deleted, so it stays traceable. A pair marked not a match is recorded and not proposed again. Skipping costs nothing and is the right answer when you need a second opinion.

Reviewing a [golden record](/mdm/golden) is a similar act with a wider effect: the golden fields grid shows one row per field and a column per source, with the kept value highlighted and the reason it was chosen beside it. Where a value is wrong, override it with a reason rather than promoting and correcting afterwards. Promoting needs the approve permission and cannot be undone.

sections.heading: When to publish survivorship
sections.text:
Publish survivorship rules when the fields that matter each have a rule, and merge review has run long enough to show the decisions are stable. Publish too early and you promote golden records built on defaults nobody chose: the health score looks better while the substance gets worse.

A sensible order: turn on matching for one object, review a hundred pairs and fix the thresholds that produced obvious noise, set survivorship for the fields downstream depends on, promote golden records for that object, and only then widen. Check [master data health](/mdm) as you go. It is built from golden-record coverage, the confidence of automatically merged pairs, how often stewardship tasks are resolved in time, and how far the sources agree with the golden record. Coverage carries the largest weight, which is another way of saying the most common cause of a poor score is not having looked.

Write-back of a golden record to SAP is its own controlled step: someone other than the requester approves each one, and where live write-back is switched off, golden values travel as a file your team loads.

sections.heading: The glossary as shared language
sections.text:
The [glossary](/mdm/glossary) defines each business term, where it lives in SAP, who owns it, which values are approved and which rules check it. Terms are drafted from the fields the rules already read, so the list starts half-written and needs people to make it true.

It is not documentation for its own sake. A steward, an owner and a report all say "supplier": the glossary is what makes those the same question. When a rule disagrees with the business definition, one of them is wrong, and that disagreement is the finding. Mark a term reviewed when you have checked its definition and owner; reviews that come due arrive as tasks in the inbox.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Decide pairs in [Match review](/mdm/golden/merge).
- Set the choices per field in [Survivorship](/mdm/survivorship).
- Check coverage and health at [Master data](/mdm).

chapters.title: Getting answers: Ask Meridian, search, tours
chapters.summary: Ask Meridian, ⌘K search, tours, what's new, shortcuts, the documentation library.

sections.text: Three habits turn Meridian from a tool you visit into a tool that answers you: ask it a question in plain words, jump anywhere from one box, and take the tour once instead of learning by accident. This chapter covers those, plus where the written answers live.

sections.heading: Ask Meridian, and what it will tell you
sections.text:
The Ask Meridian control sits at the foot of every page. Type a short question in ordinary words: which objects are weakest, what changed since the last run, how many records are still open on one rule, who holds the overdue work. It answers in sentences, with the figures underneath and a link to the page each answer came from.

The important property is where the numbers come from. Every figure in an answer is a figure Meridian already computed for the pages you can open: the same run, the same rules, the same basis. An answer lists the facts it was assembled from and carries links to the checks those facts name, so you can open what the answer rests on rather than take it on trust. When a language model is configured, it may reword those facts, and the answer is then labelled as worded from them. The model is not asked for numbers and never supplies one.

It also refuses. If your figures do not answer the question, it says so plainly and suggests what to ask instead, rather than producing a plausible sentence with an invented number in it. Partial answers are marked as covering part of the question, so you know how much of it was actually matched.

Treat it as a fast route to the right page, not as an authority. If you are going to quote a figure in a report, open the page behind the answer and quote from there: the run is named, the basis is stated, and a colleague can be sent to the same address.

Questions it handles well are comparisons, counts and changes over time. Questions it will not answer are predictions about money, judgements about people, and anything about data outside your scope: what you see is what your role and grants cover.

sections.heading: Search and jump with the command palette
sections.text:
Press Ctrl K, or `⌘K` on a Mac, anywhere. The palette lists every page your role can open; type part of a name and press Enter. It is the fastest route to a page you know exists.

It also reads what you type with fixed rules, without asking a model anything. A rule ID such as `MM003` opens that rule. An object name opens it. A record key, for example a ten-digit material number, opens that record. A severity or a dimension combined with an object opens that object's rules narrowed to them. Anything it cannot interpret opens the search page, which spans objects, rules, glossary terms, fix batches and runs, exact matches first.

A second box, in the scope bar on every page, does one job better: find a failing record by key or name. Press `/`, type two or more characters, pick a match and the record opens inside its object. It searches the failing records of the run you are viewing, so a record that passes is not listed; for that, search from the object page or the palette.

sections.heading: Tours, what is new, and the keys
sections.text:
The help menu, marked **?**, offers a guided tour on the pages that have one. Tours are per role: stewards see the queue and the record panel, leads see the verdict and the owners view, Basis sees connections, extraction and configuration loads, process analysts see discovery runs and variants. A tour moves between pages for you and skips steps whose page has nothing to show yet, so take yours after a system is connected rather than before.

Every tour can be replayed. Dismissing one counts as done; the preference page offers a reset that shows them again.

The same menu opens what is new, a short list of what changed in this version with a link to the page each item lives on. Read it after an update: features are switched on quietly, and the release note is the honest way to find out why a page looks different.

And it opens the keyboard shortcuts for the page you are on, which is also `?` pressed on the page itself. The keys worth learning first are the ones for repetitive work: `j` and `k` to move, `a` to accept a suggestion, `t` to take a record, `u` to undo. In the inbox they claim, approve and reject. Keys never fire while you are typing in a box, so nothing goes wrong by leaving the cursor where it is.

sections.heading: The written answers
sections.text:
The user guide, in the help centre, holds the full guide chapter by chapter, with a printable copy of all of them. It is written for the work, not for the product: each chapter covers one job from start to finish. Open it from the help menu or from [the user guide](/docs), and search it from the palette.

Every statistic carries a hint: hover the small mark beside a number and the definition appears, with a link to the chapter that explains it. That is deliberate, because the four counts of what fails, failing rules, rule failures, failing records and records to fix, measure different things and are routinely confused. When two people disagree about a number, check they are reading the same definition before you compare anything else.

Preferences are worth setting once, at [Me, Preferences](/me/preferences): your time zone so run times and due times read sensibly, your locale, theme and row density. They are stored on the server, so they follow you to any browser and any machine.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Read the full guide in [the user guide](/docs).
- Search across everything at [Search](/search).
- Set your time zone and density at [Preferences](/me/preferences).

chapters.title: Creating and managing users
chapters.summary: Invite, assign roles, custom roles, view-as, sessions and password rules.

sections.text: Users are the licence, the queue and the audit trail all at once. Every name on the users page is a seat, a set of grants, and the attribution on every decision that person has made. The page needs the manage users permission; add people deliberately, give them the narrowest role that lets them work, and take access away the day someone leaves.

sections.heading: Invite the person
sections.text:
Open the users page and start an invitation. You enter the email address, optionally a name, and choose one role: that role applies to every system. Under an expandable section you can add further grants for a single system or a single object instead, and you need at least one grant of either kind before the invitation can go.

The invitation is an email with a link. The person sets their own password on the join page; you never see it and you cannot set it for them. The link is single use and lasts seven days. There is no resend button anywhere on the users page, and the address cannot be invited twice while it is listed, so a lost or expired link is usually fixed by removing the entry and inviting again, which works only while nothing else refers to that account.

The users list shows how many people there are and how many have never signed in. That second number is your follow-up list.

sections.heading: Roles, and what each one is for
sections.text:
Roles come as grants, not as a field you can type into. Changing someone's role means adding or removing grants under [Roles and access](/admin/roles); the users page refuses a direct role edit and sends you there.

- **Data steward** (and the older steward name) applies values, works the fix list, maintains rules and can take or release records. Stewards land on fix work.
- **Data owner / approver** is the second pair of eyes: approve and export only. They cannot type values or take records, so they land on approvals.
- **Analyst** extracts, runs analyses and exports, but holds no apply or approve, so fix work stays hidden.
- **SAP Basis** adds system connections, credentials and field mapping to the analyst's set.
- **Programme lead / CIO** (and the older manager name) runs the programme: systems, analysis, approvals, assignment and the audit log.
- **Platform admin** (and the older admin name) is everything, including users, roles, settings, the licence and updates.
- **Auditor** reads everything, exports, and opens the audit log. **Viewer** reads only, with no export.
- **Process analyst** reads everything, runs discovery and exports as-is process models.
- **AI reviewer** is the legacy reviewer role, kept for its approval rights over proposed rules.

Older role names still work for accounts that carry them, and each keeps the rights of the modern role above. New grants are given as the modern roles.

sections.heading: Custom roles and the role matrix
sections.text:
Built-in roles are read-only. Clone one, name the copy, then tick or clear permissions in its matrix and save. A custom role can be granted for one system or one object only, which is how you give a colleague stewardship of a single plant without making them a steward everywhere. Deleting a custom role takes the access away from everyone who holds it, at every scope it was granted for; their other roles stay.

On the same page you can see a person's effective permissions per system, decide access requests people have raised, and read a history of role, grant and request changes.

The view-as switch on any home page previews the layout of another role: the arrangement changes, your permissions do not. Use it to check what a new starter will actually see before you call them.

sections.heading: Passwords, sessions and leaving
sections.text:
Passwords are short to type and long to guess: twelve characters is the only written rule, and the local policy is deliberately simple. If your organisation enforces something stricter, connect your identity provider and leave local authentication out of the path.

A forced change on first sign-in applies to the seeded bootstrap administrator account, not to invited people. Invited people choose their own password when they accept, so nothing is set on their behalf.

Changing a password signs out every other session that account holds and replaces the current one. That is the point: a stolen session dies with the old password. Password resets behave the same way.

sections.heading: Suspension, removal and the last admin
sections.text:
Untick Active to block sign-in. A suspension ends that person's live sessions immediately, keeps their name on past work, and is reversible. Removing a user deletes the row, and it asks you to type the email address first. Removal fails when the person is referenced by audit or stewardship records, which is common after any real work: suspend instead.

You cannot change your own access, and an administrator cannot demote, suspend or remove the last active admin of the tenant. Make a second person an admin before you touch the first.

Seats are counted on the licence page, which compares active users against the grant. Adding seats is done in Meridian HQ; nothing in the app buys them.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Set what each role may do in [Roles and access](/admin/roles).
- Check seats and entitlements in [Licence](/admin/licence).
- Review who changed what in [Audit log](/admin/audit).

chapters.title: Rules governance for administrators
chapters.summary: Enable, disable, re-severity, suppress, review learned rules, and what proofs guarantee.

sections.text: Rules decide what counts as a defect, so they are the one part of Meridian an administrator should not change casually. Nearly everything shipped is fixed upstream: the tenant's real power is to switch a rule off, keep a noisy one out of the score for a while, and approve or reject the rules proposed from your own data.

sections.heading: The rule ledger
sections.text:
Open the rules page. Every check an analysis can run is listed there, most failing records first, with its object, severity, pass rate, failing record count, last run and state. Filters cover object, view, severity, state, system type, check type, dimension, authority and table, and search matches the rule id, name, description and tags.

Turning a rule on or off is the only change the ledger accepts, and it needs the manage rules permission. There is no inline switch: because the change moves every later score, each toggle asks first and says what happens. Turning one off means the next analysis stops checking it and its failures no longer count; turning it on reverses both. The message afterwards offers undo, and that undo holds only if nobody has changed the rule since. A rule you switch off stays off until you switch it back, but a later push from HQ can overwrite the flag: the toggle is for immediate relief on a noisy rule between syncs, not permanent reconfiguration. Without the permission, the library is read-only and says so.

sections.heading: What HQ controls
sections.text:
Severity is not yours to set. Each licence validation copies HQ's catalogue into the tenant: rule id, name, description, module, category, severity, enabled flag, conditions, thresholds and tags. Analysis reads that copy alongside the shipped rules, so a re-severity request goes to Meridian HQ, where the catalogue is maintained.

The one tenant-side route that rewrites a rule is a rule version: a partial override merged over the shipped definition. Versions are listed on the rule's own page with their state and who approved them, and moving a version between states is a page control. Writing one is still an API call rather than a button, under the manage rules permission. That is where the maker-checker sits: a draft goes to review under manage rules, and only a reviewer holding approve, or the AI reviewer permission, can activate it. The author cannot approve their own version, and the earlier active version retires as the new one takes effect, from the next analysis run. Where HQ's catalogue carries a severity for that rule, the catalogue's value is what the analysis uses, whatever the override says.

sections.heading: Suppressions, and the difference from disabling
sections.text:
A suppression keeps a rule, or one record of it, out of the score until it expires. They are made from a finding rather than from the ledger, and the Suppressions tab lists them with scope, reason, expiry, who made it and an **End now** action for anyone with the approve permission. Ending one takes effect on the next run.

The difference is worth respecting. Disabling is a tenant decision about the rule; a suppression is a decision about a score, time-boxed and attributed, which is what makes it defensible in an audit. An expired suppression simply stops being read.

sections.heading: Approving what your own data suggests
sections.text:
Learned rules are patterns your data follows for at least nine in ten records. Mining runs after each analysis and can be started by hand from the learned rules page. Approving one creates a live rule from the next run at the severity you pick; rejecting records the decision. Approving needs approve or the AI reviewer permission, and rejecting is also open to whoever maintains rules.

Rule drafts holds the proposals the AI makes from steward corrections, including match rules; someone with the AI review permission approves or rejects each with a reason. Drafted rules are dry-run against an analysed version before they are published.

Every shipped and generated rule is proven before it reaches you: the test suite gives each one a record it fails and a record it passes. A rule that cannot fail tests nothing, and one that cannot pass condemns every record. That proof runs in CI.

sections.heading: Depth and scoring
sections.text:
The rules page carries a coverage table by object: rules total, how many are configuration-aware, how many apply by default, how many do not apply, and how many applicable rules pass. It is measured on a finished run, so it says nothing before the first one. Per object, that object's rules tab ranks its checks by failing records and drills through to the records.

Scoring is where the numbers are weighted. Dimension weights must sum to one before they save, and the page shows a reweighted preview of the latest run beside the current score, warning that the preview ignores caps. Caps are fixed: a critical rule failing beyond its tolerance caps that object at 85, two or more at 70. Saved weights apply from the next analysis run. The same page holds the alert thresholds, the per-object score floors and the costs that turn defects into money, where a feature with no price is left out of value at risk rather than guessed at.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Write and dry-run a rule in [Authoring rules](/rules/drafts).
- Review what your data suggests at [Learned rules](/rules/learned).
- Set weights and alert thresholds at [Scoring](/rules/scoring).

chapters.title: Executing runs: analysis, discovery and baselines
chapters.summary: Schedule and scope runs, watch jobs, pin baselines, compare versions, handle failures.

sections.text: A run is a measurement, taken at a moment, of the records Meridian holds. Every score, queue and comparison downstream reads it, so the craft is starting the right one, watching it finish, and pinning the one that marks your baseline.

sections.heading: What a run does, in order
sections.text:
Extraction reads the tables behind the objects you selected, filtered by the scope you set, and stores them as a version; the connection is read-only, so nothing is written back to SAP. The checks then run over that stored data: each rule applying to the object is evaluated, findings and failing records are written, and every object is scored into dimension scores and its data quality score. As scoring finishes Meridian builds the work list, routes new issues to owners, starts their clocks, and compares the run with the system's pinned baseline. Summaries and remediation text come afterwards, which is why a run can finish as scored and move again later.

Statuses mean different things: extracted is stored but unchecked; complete and its enriched variants have findings to read; partial means some checks were skipped; failed has nothing to read.

Re-running an analysis over data you already extracted is a separate action, on the run page and the system page. It re-checks the stored records with the current rules, replaces the findings, and keeps the run's name, baseline and history. It is the cheap way to test a rule change: no SAP read.

sections.heading: Scopes, periods and schedules
sections.text:
Open a system and choose Extract. Tick the objects, then narrow the read: company codes, plants, sales or purchasing organisations where the object carries them, a document date window where it has one, and an option to skip records flagged for deletion. Organisational filters restrict every table carrying that field, and general data without it is read in full so no record loses its context. Skipping deletion-flagged records reads faster, but inactive data is itself a finding, so leave it off for a true score.
