The confirmation names the system, the objects and the scope: the last checkpoint before a read that can take an hour.

Scheduled extracts pull an object again on a timetable: pick the object, a preset or a custom five-field cron, and full download or changes only. Times show in the tenant time zone and due runs start within five minutes. Changes only re-reads what SAP's change log says moved, with a full download at least weekly so a gap in the log cannot hide.

sections.heading: Jobs, retries and failed extractions
sections.text:
The jobs page holds the newest two hundred extractions, analyses, uploads, configuration loads and discovery runs with status, duration, rows and a detail line. Expand a failed job for the error in one sentence, the next step, and the raw text underneath. Retry repeats a failed extraction, analysis, configuration load or discovery run, and needs the permission that starting it needed; an extraction a discovery run chained cannot be repeated there and sends you back to the system's Extract drawer. The run page's steps tab lists every step with its own status.

Read failures by cause. A sign-in refusal is credentials. Unreachable is host, port or route. A refused authorisation means the connection user cannot read one of the tables, which is a request to your SAP team. A missing library means the SAP connector is not on the worker. A timeout means the read was too big for the window: retry at a quieter time, take fewer objects, or use changes only.

sections.heading: Baselines and the regression monitor
sections.text:
Pin the run taken just after a clean-up as the baseline, from the run page or the progress toolbar. Every newer run of that system is then diffed against it, rule by rule. Records failing now that passed in the baseline are regressions: they are counted on the run, they raise a notification, and they are drafted into a new fix batch named for the day. Someone still has to accept its proposals and a second person approve it; Meridian never posts to SAP. Unpinning returns later runs to comparing against the previous run.

Comparing two specific runs is separate: select two in the runs list, or use compare with previous or compare with baseline on a run page. Both show what is new, what is fixed and what still fails, per rule and per record.

sections.heading: Discovery, and running out of memory
sections.text:
Discovery reads the document and change tables of a business process and reconstructs how it ran, reporting coverage, fitness, variants and durations. Start it from a process page, pick the processes and, on a full run, a period start. A process your licence does not entitle is listed greyed out with "not in this licence", and no retry changes that. A full run takes from a few minutes to two hours, and only one discovery chain runs against a system at a time.

Memory guards are sizing feedback, not data faults. A discovery run over budget tells you to narrow the period. An extraction that would need more memory than the worker has says so before allocating, and names the two fixes: more worker memory, or a narrower object. Shorten the window, split the object across runs, or move it to changes only, and note the decision on the object page.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Manage systems, extracts and schedules at [Systems](/systems).
- Watch and retry jobs at [Jobs](/admin/jobs).
- Read run history and comparisons at [Runs](/runs).

chapters.title: Assigning tasks to users
chapters.summary: Object owners, queues, digests, triage and SLA settings that route the work.

sections.text: Work reaches people through three things working together: ownership set on objects and rules, triage rules that route new issues, and queues people can see. Get those right and the fix list organises itself week after week. Get them wrong and every steward works on whatever they noticed first.

sections.heading: Say who owns what
sections.text:
Ownership is set on the object page, where an owner and a steward can be chosen from the active users of this tenant. The same two fields sit on a rule page under its lineage and ownership card, so a rule that keeps causing arguments has a name against it. Changing ownership needs the assign permission; without it the page shows who holds the role and offers nothing to change.

Owners matter beyond the label. When no assignment rule matches, routing falls through in a fixed order: the rule's owner, then the object's owner, then the steward named on the glossary term, then the tenant's fallback user. An object with no owner is a queue with no bottom.

sections.heading: How a new issue finds a person
sections.text:
After each analysis, and again on a five-minute sweep, unassigned issues are put through your assignment rules in order. The first match wins: a rule can narrow on severity, object, rule id, dimension, company code, plant or sales organisation, and it sends what matches to a team or a named person. Inside a team, work is spread either round robin or to whoever is least loaded, which is the setting that matters when one steward is on leave.

Anything unmatched goes to the fallback chain above, which is why the fallback user on the working calendar is worth setting deliberately: it is the person who quietly receives everything your rules do not describe.

Assignment starts a clock. An issue with no deadline takes its acknowledge and resolve times from the SLA policy matching its severity, and optionally its object, counted in business hours against your working calendar. Waiting states pause the clock, and leaving one moves the deadlines by the time spent waiting. At-risk and breached each raise one notification, never a repeat every sweep.

sections.heading: The queues people actually work from
sections.text: Fix work is where record-level work happens. A steward takes records for themselves, releases them, or hands one to a named colleague from the record panel; a whole selection can be taken at once. The Inbox holds approvals, exceptions and review tasks with the same claim, reassign and release actions, and exceptions carry their own deadlines and escalation. Keep the model simple: route by rule and severity, let people claim within that, and reserve named assignment for items that genuinely need one specific person.

sections.heading: Configure it on the triage page
sections.text:
The triage page holds teams, assignment rules, SLA policies and the working calendar. Teams take a name, a strategy, a lead and members, and show their open items. Assignment rules can be switched off and moved up or down, because the order is the policy. SLA policies show acknowledge and resolve times, the at-risk share and whether the clock counts business or calendar hours; deleting an override sends that severity back to the default. The calendar sets the time zone, work days, hours, holidays and the fallback user, and it warns before changing the time zone because extraction schedules move with it.

Teams, rules and SLAs need the manage rules permission; the calendar needs manage settings. Everyone can read them.

sections.heading: Tell people what they are holding
sections.text:
The owners view ranks people by the score of the records assigned to them, with open issues by severity, movement over the last seven days, what each owner fixed and how old their oldest item is. Each row opens that person's inbox. The same page sends the weekly digest on demand, for one owner or for everyone, which writes the notification without changing the schedule; someone who has chosen their own digest frequency in their preferences is served by that instead.

Alert channels carry the same news out of the app: email, Slack, Teams or a signed webhook, each with a digest frequency, an option to send new critical findings immediately, and a test you can send before you trust it. Alerts carry counts, rule ids and links, never record values, which is what makes them safe on a shared channel.

Report schedules are a lighter form of the same idea: a named report on a daily, weekly or monthly cadence at a set time in a chosen zone, sent to up to fifty users and up to twenty alert channels. Recipients must be active and hold the export permission, or the schedule is refused.

sections.heading: Balance the load before it piles up
sections.text:
The progress view has a workload table: open rule failures, critical count and overdue items per person, with an explicit row for nobody yet. That last row is the one to read first, because unassigned work is not late, it is invisible. Decisions per person sit beside it, so a large backlog held by someone making no decisions reads differently from the same backlog worked steadily.

Move work where the evidence says to: an assignment rule for the object that keeps landing on one person, an SLA override for a severity your calendar cannot meet, and a scheduled report so the numbers arrive without anyone asking.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Set teams, routing and deadlines at [Triage](/admin/triage).
- Read the workload table in [Progress](/insights/progress).
- Send owners their digest from [Owners](/insights/owners).

chapters.title: Administrator best practices
chapters.summary: Licence, alerts, audit, cost model, retention, updates, health — and a weekly rhythm.

sections.text:
Nothing in Meridian needs a daily inspection. What it needs is a rhythm: one pass a week through the things that fail quietly, and a short order to check them in when something looks wrong.

Start with the licence, then health, then jobs, then what alerted, then the audit trail and the retention policy you set. Fifteen minutes, in that order.

sections.heading: Licence, seats and version
sections.text:
The licence page shows tenant, tier, status, seats in use against the seats granted, days remaining, the renewal date, when the deployment last validated, and the language-model tier the licence entitles. Validate now asks Meridian HQ immediately instead of waiting for the six-hourly check. Renewals and extra seats are handled in Meridian HQ, not here, and the deployment keeps its data either way; a renewal appears after the next check. Watch the seat line, which warns as the grant runs out.

The same page shows the version running and, for a platform administrator, whether an update is available. Updating restarts Meridian for everyone and rolls back on its own if a step fails; the update script on the server takes a rollback argument too. Plan it like any other change window.

sections.heading: Connections, and what the states mean
sections.text:
Health is a badge on each system: healthy, degraded, unreachable, sign-in refused, or not tested. Each carries a reason in words, with the raw check text behind it, and each system offers a connection test that names what it found. Sign-in refused is credentials. Unreachable is host, port or route. Degraded usually means a last read that partly failed.

Test the connection before you chase a score. A system whose credentials changed and was never re-tested reads exactly like a healthy one, and trusting a stale badge is the fastest way to lose an afternoon.

sections.heading: Alerts worth wiring
sections.text:
Four events fire an outbound alert, and the code fires exactly those: an object's score falling further than your drop threshold, new critical rules failing, exception SLA breaches, and records failing again since the pinned baseline. Thresholds and per-object score floors sit on the scoring page; channels sit under notifications.

Set the drop threshold from what your own runs actually do, not from a round number: too tight and every delta extract wakes the channel, too loose and a genuine collapse arrives in Friday's digest. Put critical findings on immediate delivery and everything else on a digest, and send a test when you add a channel. Alerts carry counts, rule ids and links, never record values, which is what makes them safe on a shared channel.

sections.heading: The audit trail
sections.text:
Every change made through the API is recorded, so the audit log answers who, what, when and from where, with the request behind it when you expand a row. There are three views: the full log, the calls made to the language model with their outcome, and user changes alone. Filter by person, date window or the kind of change, and export as CSV or XLSX with those filters applied, which is what an auditor asks for.

Read the AI view as a health signal too. A run of failures or skipped calls means narrative is silently absent from reports, and the log tells you before your lead does.

sections.heading: Pricing, so the money is yours
sections.text:
Two panels carry the cost model. Under settings you price risk and return: the currency, the monthly subscription, the unit cost of each business-impact defect type with its factor and mitigated share, and the impact of each configuration finding type. Under scoring you price the record: cost per blocked record by severity, and a value per blocked record for each SAP feature you want in value at risk.

Only your own numbers appear. A feature with no value is left out of value at risk rather than given an invented one, and without a subscription the return states the cost avoided with no multiple attached. Changing the currency relabels amounts; it does not convert them, so restate them.

sections.heading: Retention and backups
sections.text:
Retention is a policy plus a nightly task: how long runs, reports and audit rows are kept, how many runs per system are always kept, and whether the pinned baseline is protected. Only archived runs are ever purged, and golden records, rules, glossary terms and contracts are never touched. Preview before you save, watch the purge log, and remember that real deletes begin only after a week of dry runs under the current policy. A whole-tenant deletion is a separate, deliberately slow operation, and it returns a certificate.

Backups are your own: this deployment keeps its state in named volumes for the database and for object storage. Snapshot both on one schedule, keep a copy off the host, and restore one to prove it works before you need it.

sections.heading: When something looks wrong
sections.text:
Check in this order, and stop as soon as an answer appears.

1. Jobs: is a run failed, and what does its error sentence say? Read the cause, fix it, retry the job.
2. System health: is the connection in the state its last test reported, and has the configuration been loaded since the SAP change?
3. Audit: did someone change a rule, a grant or a threshold at the moment the number moved?

Most surprises end at step three.

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
- Read entitlements and version at [Licence](/admin/licence).
- Manage connections and tests at [Systems](/systems).
- Set channels and retention at [Settings](/admin/settings).

chapters.title: Welcome to Meridian
chapters.summary: Meridian checks your SAP data against rules. It lists every record that fails and says why. Where it can, it suggests the right value. It routes each fix through a second person's approval and out to

sections.text:
Meridian checks your SAP data against rules. It lists every record that fails and says why. Where it can, it suggests the right value. It routes each fix through a second person's approval and out to SAP as a load file. It then tracks progress run by run until the data is clean.

This guide is written for the people who do that work: data stewards who clean records, data owners who approve them, leads who follow progress, and the analysts and administrators who keep Meridian running. Start with this chapter, then read [Key concepts](/docs?page=concepts) and [Fix work](/docs?page=fix).

sections.heading: Your data stays with you
sections.text:
Meridian runs inside your organisation's own environment. SAP data, findings and reports are stored there and do not leave it. The only call Meridian makes to the outside on its own is licence validation, which carries no SAP data.

Every score, count and suggested value comes from a fixed rule, so the same data always gives the same result. The built-in language model receives summaries of findings for written commentary, never raw SAP records, and any text it writes is labelled as such.

sections.heading: Signing in
sections.text:
Accounts are created by an administrator. There is no self sign-up.

1. Open the invitation email and follow its link. The **Join Meridian** page asks you to choose a password.
2. On the sign-in page, enter your **Work email** and **Password**, then select **Sign in**.
3. Meridian opens the page for your role, or the page you were trying to reach.

Where you land depends on your role. Data stewards land on **Fix work**. Data owners and approvers land on **Inbox**, **Approvals**. Leads, analysts, administrators, auditors and viewers land on the data lead Home page, SAP Basis on the Basis Home page and process analysts on the process Home page. The Meridian mark at the left of the index bar always brings you back to your Home page. If you forget your password, select **Forgot password?** and follow the link in the email.

sections.heading: The screen
sections.text:
Every page has the same frame. There is no sidebar.

### The index bar

The top row is the index bar. From left to right:

- The Meridian mark, which opens your Home page.
- The pills, the places you work from every day. Each role has its own strip, in the order it works:
  - Leads, analysts, administrators, auditors and viewers: **Home**, **Objects**, **Fix work**, **Inbox**, **Progress** and **Runs**.
  - Data stewards: **Fix work**, **Inbox**, **Objects**, **Match review**, **Runs** and **Progress**.
  - Data owners and approvers: **Approvals**, **Inbox**, **Objects**, **Fix work**, **Progress** and **Runs**.
  - SAP Basis: **Systems**, **Jobs**, **Runs**, **Inbox** and **Objects**.
  - Process analysts: **Processes**, **Objects**, **Runs**, **Progress** and **Inbox**.

  **Fix work** carries the number of records to fix (no number appears until a run's work list is built), and **Inbox** the number of open stewardship tasks. You see only the pills your role allows.
- **More**, which opens every other page you may use, grouped as **Analysis**, **Master data**, **Rules**, **Data in** and **Admin**. A page your role's strip leaves out, such as **Fix work** for a process analyst, is listed first. Press Escape or select outside the panel to close it.
- On the right: **Search or jump to...** (Ctrl K, or ⌘K on a Mac), the jobs tray, the **To do** flag with the number of critical and high items waiting for you (see [To do](/docs?page=todo)), the notification bell, the help menu (**?**) and your user menu.

### The scope bar

Under the index bar is the scope bar. It names the page you are on and, on the right, holds two controls you will use all day:

- **Search**: type a record key or a name, pick one of the failing records it matches, and the record opens in its object. Press `/` from anywhere to open the search.
- **Run**: the run every screen shows. **Latest run** follows the newest finished run. Pick an older run and Meridian keeps it as you move between screens, in this browser, until you pick **Latest run** again.

When your access is limited to one system or object, a pill such as "Scoped: PRD ECC, Material master" sits beside them.

### The help menu

The **?** button offers **Tour this page** (where a guided tour exists), **Keyboard shortcuts**, **What's new**, **Help centre** and **Report a problem**. The **Help centre** is the one place for help: guides for the work each role does, training recordings where one exists, and this user guide, chapter by chapter. In the user guide, **Download PDF** gives you a printable copy of every chapter.

sections.heading: Your first day
sections.text:
- **Data steward**: open **Fix work**, switch on **Mine** or pick an object, and work the list from the top. See [Fix work](/docs?page=fix).
- **Data owner or approver**: you land on **Inbox**, **Approvals**: approve the fix batches your stewards prepared and the SAP write-backs others requested. See [Approvals and export](/docs?page=approvals).
- **Lead**: open **Progress** to see how fast the backlog is falling and what slows it. See [Progress](/docs?page=progress).
- **SAP Basis**: open **Systems** to connect a system and run the first extraction. See [Data in](/docs?page=data-in).
- **Analyst**: open **More**, **Data in**, **Systems** to connect a system and run the first extraction, or **Import file** to load an export. See [Data in](/docs?page=data-in).

sections.heading: Good to know
sections.text:
- Because the run is in the page address, a link you copy shows a colleague the same numbers.
- Your preferences, such as theme and row density, are under the user menu and follow you to any browser.

sections.text:

- [Roles and access](/docs?page=roles)
- [Fix work](/docs?page=fix)
- [Keyboard shortcuts and search](/docs?page=shortcuts)

chapters.title: Key concepts
chapters.summary: This chapter explains the words every other chapter uses: run, object, rule, issue, record, suggestion, fix batch and the six statuses a record moves through. It ends with how the data quality score i

sections.text: This chapter explains the words every other chapter uses: run, object, rule, issue, record, suggestion, fix batch and the six statuses a record moves through. It ends with how the data quality score is built. Read it once before you rely on a number in Meridian.

sections.heading: Run
sections.text:
A run is one measurement of your data at a point in time. Meridian creates a run each time it extracts data from a system or you import a file. The rules then run over that data, and every score, failing record and suggestion belongs to that run.

- A run is finished when its analysis completes. Every screen shows finished runs only.
- The **Run** picker in the scope bar chooses the run for every screen. **Latest run** always follows the newest finished run.
- Runs are compared only with runs of the same source, called the run's lineage. Every extraction from one system is one lineage; imported files are grouped by the objects they carry.
- A baseline is a run you pin as the reference for later runs, such as the run after a clean-up.

Each finished run also gets a work list: the failing records ranked worst first, with their statuses. Fix work reads that list. Runs from before the work list existed have none until someone builds it (see [Troubleshooting](/docs?page=troubleshooting)).

sections.heading: Object
sections.text: An object is one area of SAP data that Meridian measures as a whole, such as Material master, Business partner, Accounts payable or eWMS stock. Each object has its own rules, its own score and a verdict: **Go**, **At risk** or **No-go**. See [Objects](/docs?page=objects).

sections.heading: Check and rule
sections.text: A rule, also called a check, is one fixed test on the data, with an ID such as `MM001`. Each rule has a dimension, a severity (critical, high, medium or low), the field it reads, a plain message that says what is wrong, and usually an instruction for fixing it. The same data always gives the same result. See [Rules](/docs?page=rules).

sections.heading: Record
sections.text: A record is one row a rule judges, such as one material, one vendor or one sales order line. It is identified by its record key, built from its SAP key fields, for example `MATNR=000000000010001234`. Where the data carries a name, Meridian shows the name first and the key under it.

sections.heading: Issue
sections.text: An issue is one rule that one record fails. A record can have several issues: a vendor may lack a tax number and carry an invalid bank key at the same time. In Fix work, the **Issues** list on the left groups the issues by rule, so you can work one problem across many records, and the record panel lists every issue of the record you picked.

sections.heading: Suggestion
sections.text:
A suggestion is the value Meridian proposes for a failing field. It comes from one of three places, and the record panel says which:

- **Rule fix, checked against the rule**: the rule's own correction, tested by running the rule again on the new value.
- **The rule's fix for this value**: a fixed mapping from a known bad value to the right one.
- **Cleaning engine**: a proposal from the cleaning queue, with its confidence.

Not every issue has a suggestion. When there is none, you enter the value yourself.

sections.heading: Fix batch
sections.text: A fix batch is a set of record-level corrections that are approved and exported together. When you accept a suggestion or enter a value in Fix work, it goes into your own draft batch, named "Fixes by" and your name. A second person must approve the batch: the person who drafted it can neither approve nor export it. The approved batch is exported as a load file for SAP. See [Approvals and export](/docs?page=approvals).

sections.heading: The six statuses
sections.text:
Every failing record in the work list has one status:

1. **To fix**: nobody has decided a value yet.
2. **Fix proposed**: a value waits in a draft fix batch for a second person to approve.
3. **Approved**: the batch is approved and waits to be exported for the SAP load.
4. **Sent to SAP**: the batch was exported; the next run confirms the fix.
5. **Not an issue**: someone with the approve permission signed it off as an exception, with a reason.
6. **Fixed**: a later run showed the record passing.

The first four are open work. **Still open** in a status filter means any of them. A record whose value was sent to SAP but that the next run still finds failing goes back to **To fix**, with a warning that says so.

sections.heading: The data quality score
sections.text: The data quality score (DQS) runs from 0 to 100. Each rule gives a record-level pass rate; severity scales the failing share; rules are averaged into six dimensions (completeness and accuracy 25% each, consistency 20%, timeliness, uniqueness and validity 10% each); and the dimensions are weighted into the object's score. One critical rule failing over tolerance caps the score at 85, two or more at 70. The weights can be changed per tenant on **Scoring and alerts**.

chapters.title: Roles and access
chapters.summary: Your role decides which pages you see and what you can change on them. This chapter explains the six permissions that matter for fixing data, lists every role with what it sees and can do, and shows h

sections.text: Your role decides which pages you see and what you can change on them. This chapter explains the six permissions that matter for fixing data, lists every role with what it sees and can do, and shows how to ask for more access.

sections.heading: How access works
sections.text:
- Every user has one main role, for every system and object.
- An administrator can add grants: a further role for one system, one object, or one object on one system. What you can do is the sum of your main role and every grant that covers the record in front of you.
- Pages and buttons you cannot use are hidden, so the menus never offer a dead end. The server checks the same permissions on every request.
- A grant can carry an expiry date. It stops working that day, and the access review lists the ones that end within 30 days.
- Your licence can switch pages off for every role.
- Someone who signs in through your identity provider for the first time is a viewer with no grants until an administrator gives them access.

sections.heading: The six permissions behind fixing data
sections.text:
- **view**: open pages and read records, scores and findings. Every role has it.
- **apply**: accept a suggestion, enter a value, set one value for a whole issue, undo a decision and import a fix sheet. Values go into your own draft fix batch.
- **approve**: mark a record **Not an issue** or **Accept risk**, withdraw a sign-off, approve a fix batch, accept high-confidence proposals in a batch, and merge duplicates.
- **assign**: take a record or release it, for yourself or in bulk.
- **analyse**: run analyses, build a run's work list, pin a baseline, and add comments on a record.
- **export**: download the fix sheet, export an approved batch for the SAP load, and download reports.

**Fix work** appears for every role that holds apply or approve.

sections.heading: The roles
sections.text:
### Data steward

The person who cleans the data. Holds view, apply, approve, assign, analyse and export, and may also maintain rules, contracts and the glossary. Lands on **Fix work**. A steward can do everything in Fix work, but cannot approve or export a batch they drafted themselves.

### Data owner / approver

The second pair of eyes. Holds view, approve and export. Lands on **Inbox**, **Approvals**, where they approve the fix batches stewards prepared and the SAP write-backs others requested. In **Fix work** they sign off records as **Not an issue** or **Accept risk**, and export approved batches. They cannot enter values, take records or comment.

### Programme lead / CIO

Runs the programme. Holds view, apply, approve, assign, analyse and export, plus connecting systems, editing master data and reading the audit log. Lands on the data lead Home page and usually works from **Progress**.

### Platform admin

Full access, including users and roles, rules, settings, the licence and updates. Lands on the data lead Home page.

### Analyst

Imports files, extracts, runs analyses and exports. Holds view, analyse and export, but neither apply nor approve, so **Fix work** is hidden. An analyst can still open an object's **Records to fix** tab and read each record, and builds a run's work list when one is missing.

### SAP Basis / integration admin

Everything the analyst can do, plus connecting and editing SAP systems and their credentials, and field mapping. Lands on the Basis Home page.

### Auditor, viewer and process analyst

- **Auditor**: read everything, export, and read the audit log.
- **Viewer**: read only. On report pages the export button becomes **Print**.
- **Process analyst**: read everything, run process discovery and export as-is process models. Lands on the process Home page.

Older role names (Admin, Manager, Steward, Approver, AI reviewer) still work and carry the rights of the matching role above.

sections.heading: See what a role can do
sections.text: Administrators do not have to guess. Open **Roles and access**, then **Matrix** for a grid of what every role may do on each kind of data; built-in roles are read only, so clone one to change it. Select a role to read **What this role sees**: the pages a person holding only that role could open. It is a preview, and nobody is impersonated. **Show legacy actions** adds the older permission names.

sections.heading: What each role sees
sections.text:
- **Objects**, **Progress** and **Inbox**: every role.
- **Fix work** and **What-if**: roles with apply or approve (Platform admin, Programme lead, Data steward, Data owner).
- **Inbox**, **Exceptions**: roles with approve or assign.
- **More**, **Analysis**, **Master data**, **Rules** and **Data in**, **Systems**: every role.
- **Import file**: roles that may upload. **Migration**: roles with analyse.
- **Rules**, **Drafts**: roles that maintain rules (Platform admin, Data steward).
- **Users**, **Sign-in** and **Roles and access**: Platform admin. **Audit log**: Platform admin, Programme lead and Auditor. **Alerts**: roles that manage settings.

Tables follow the same rule: a role that can change nothing gets no selection boxes and no bulk actions. In the record panel such a role reads "Your role can view this record. Fixing it needs the apply permission."

sections.heading: Scoped access
sections.text: A grant for one system or object counts only on records of that system or object; elsewhere your main role applies. When any grant is scoped, the scope bar shows a pill such as "Scoped: PRD ECC, Material master", with "+2" for two more.

sections.heading: Grants, expiry and review
sections.text: On **Users & scopes**, an administrator adds a grant by choosing a role, a system, a module (blank for all) and an optional **Expires** date. Before the grant is saved, a preview states what changes, including that it stops working on its expiry date. **Effective permissions** shows the sum of a person's main role and every grant. **Expiring within 30 days** lists the people whose grants end soon so access is reviewed instead of lingering. Removing a grant takes effect at once. Every change is in the **History** tab and the audit log.

sections.heading: What the To do list shows you
sections.text: The [To do](/docs?page=todo) list follows the same grants. You see an item only when you hold the permission to act on it, on that system and object. Admin chores, such as access requests, invitations, seats and expiring grants, need the permission to manage users everywhere.

sections.heading: How to ask for access
sections.text:
1. Select **Request access** beside a button your role does not allow.
2. Check the **Resource**, **Action** and **Scope** Meridian filled in, and write a **Reason**.
3. Select **Send request**. An administrator grants or declines it on **Roles and access**. See [Administration](/docs?page=admin).

chapters.title: To do
chapters.summary: The To do list is the one place that says what needs a person now. It gathers failed connections, late checks, rules that started failing, work waiting for approval, overdue records and the admin chor

sections.text: The To do list is the one place that says what needs a person now. It gathers failed connections, late checks, rules that started failing, work waiting for approval, overdue records and the admin chores that pile up, ranks them, and gives each one a single button that opens the page where it is fixed. You do not have to know which page to check: open the list and work down it.

sections.heading: Where it appears
sections.text:
- **The flag in the index bar.** Next to the notification bell sits a flag labelled **To do**. Its badge counts the items that need a person soon: the critical and the high ones. The badge turns red when any of them is critical and is grey otherwise. It is absent while the number loads and when it is zero, so it never shows a number you may not act on. Select the flag to open the full list.
- **Your home page.** A **To do** card shows your five top items, each with its action, and **All** followed by the number opens the full list. The main button on the home page opens the top item when it is blocked work, a regression or a freshness problem; otherwise the home page keeps its usual button. When nothing waits, the card says so.
- **An object page.** A **To do** card under the header lists only the items about that object, and stays out of the way when there are none. **All** opens the list filtered to the object.
- **The [To do](/attention) page.** The whole list: severity, what needs a person, the object and system, how long it has been waiting, a count and the action.

The list is built once a minute for your organisation and filtered for you, and the page prints the time it was built. After you fix something, the item may stay a few seconds until the next build.

sections.heading: How items are ranked
sections.text:
Items are ordered by five priority tiers, then by severity within a tier, then by how many records or things are affected, then by how long they have waited. There are no weights to tune.

1. **Blocked work.** Something stops other people working: a system that cannot connect, or fix batches waiting for approval.
2. **Data regressions.** A rule that passed now fails, or a process fits its expected flow worse than before.
3. **Freshness.** An object is stale, a schedule failed or missed its slot, a job failed, or a process needs to be mined again.
4. **Hygiene.** Overdue records, inbox items past their time, objects with a No-go verdict, configuration that is missing or has drifted, rules waiting for review and data contracts that were breached.
5. **Admin.** Access requests, invitations nobody accepted, seats running out, grants about to expire, people who have not signed in for a long time and licence reminders.

The page has two filter rows. **Priority** shows one tier. **Kind** shows one sort of item, such as **Regressions** or **Failed schedules**; it appears when more than one kind is present. The filters are part of the address, so you can share a link to a filtered list.

sections.heading: What you see depends on your role and scope
sections.text:
Every item needs a particular permission to act on, and you see an item only when you hold that permission where the item is.

- A **data steward** sees regressions and overdue records on their own objects, and work they can fix.
- A **data owner** or approver sees the approvals waiting for them.
- A **programme lead** or **analyst** sees data items across everything they may reach, and the checks they can re-run.
- **SAP Basis** sees failed connections, failed or missed schedules, missing configuration and failed process discovery.
- A **process analyst** sees process items: fitness drops, stale discovery and failed runs.
- Admin items, such as access requests and seats, need the permission to manage users across the whole organisation.
- A **viewer** or **auditor** sees items to read, but nothing they cannot act on.

If you hold access only to one system or one object, your list shows only that slice. An empty list says "Nothing in your scope needs a person now" and names your scope, for example "Material master on one system". If you expected an item, check that your grant covers it under [Roles and access](/docs?page=roles).

sections.heading: Every item opens its fix
sections.text:
The button at the end of each row is the action, and it opens the exact page where the problem is solved, already filtered.

- **Review records** opens Fix work on the records that started failing since the baseline.
- **Re-check now**, **Retry** and **Open job** act on the check or the job that is late or failed.
- **Open schedules** and **Open system** go to the system's schedules or health.
- **Review approvals** opens the approvals in the Inbox.
- **Fix overdue records** opens the overdue records in Fix work.
- **Review requests**, **Review invitations**, **Open licence**, **Review grants** and **Review users** open the matching admin page.

A row also opens when you select anywhere on it. Every item has exactly one button, and an item you have no permission to act on is not in your list.

sections.heading: What leaves the list
sections.text: An item disappears when its cause is gone: the connection works, the check ran, the rule passes, the batch was approved. A paused schedule never creates an item, because a pause is a decision. Items you cannot act on are never hidden behind a count; they are not in your list at all.

chapters.title: Fix work
chapters.summary: Fix work is where failing records get cleaned. It lists every record that fails a check in the chosen run, worst first, says what is wrong with each one and what the value should be, and puts your dec

sections.text:
Fix work is where failing records get cleaned. It lists every record that fails a check in the chosen run, worst first, says what is wrong with each one and what the value should be, and puts your decisions into a fix batch that a second person approves before anything goes to SAP. Data stewards start here every day; data owners use it to sign records off and approve batches.

Open it with the **Fix work** pill in the index bar. The page is titled **Fix** and has two tabs: **Records to fix** and **Batches and export**. This chapter covers **Records to fix**, including the values Meridian suggests; the batches are in [Approvals and export](/docs?page=approvals). Checking whether clean data stays clean is no longer a tab here: it is per object, in [Monitoring](/docs?page=monitoring). Batches are approved in **Inbox**, **Approvals**, and duplicate pairs are reviewed in **Master data**, **Match review**.

Fix work is the one place to fix a failing record: the Inbox's old **Issues** tab moved here, and `/inbox?kind=issues` opens Fix work on your own records (**Mine**). On the record panel, **Take it** or **Release** the record, hand it to a colleague with **Assign to**, and mark an issue **Fixed in SAP** when you corrected it in SAP itself; the next run confirms it, or reopens it if the record still fails. Taking, assigning and **Fixed in SAP** need the assign permission.

sections.heading: Step 1: pick the run
sections.text:
The list belongs to one run. Use **Run** in the scope bar: **Latest run** follows the newest finished run, or pick an older one. Your choice stays as you move to Objects, Progress and back.

If no run has finished yet the page reads **No finished run yet**. If the run has no work list, a notice reads **This run's work list is not built yet**; see [Troubleshooting](/docs?page=troubleshooting).

sections.heading: Step 2: find your records
sections.text:
Four figures sit at the top. Each one filters the list when you select it:

- **Records to fix**: distinct records that still need a decision, however many rules they fail, with how many issues across how many objects.
- **Critical records**: records with a critical issue. These block SAP processes.
- **With a suggested value**: records you can accept in one step.
- **Overdue records**: records past their due date.

Under them are the filters: **Object**, **Severity**, **Status** (**Still open** by default, or one of the six statuses), the **Mine** switch for records assigned to you, the **Has a suggestion** switch, and **Find a record by key or name** (type, then press Enter). Every active filter shows as a chip, including **New since** followed by a date; select a chip to remove it, or **Clear filters**.

The screen then has three panes:

1. **Issues**, on the left: **Every issue**, then one row per rule that fails, worst first, with its message, the number of open records, the object and field, and how many have a suggested value. Pick one to work a single problem.
2. **Records to fix**, in the middle: the records, worst first, 50 at a time (**Show 50 more**). Each row shows the name or key, the main problem and "and N more issues", the status, the number of suggested values, an **Overdue** or **Due today** pill, the assignee and the object.
3. The record panel, on the right, for the record you picked. The first record is picked for you.

sections.heading: Step 3: read the record panel
sections.text:
The panel heads with the record's name and key, its object, how many checks it fails and its status. **Full record** opens the record's page under Objects.

For each issue it shows the message, the field and rule ID, the status, then:

- **Now**: the value the record holds. An empty value reads "blank"; a field the record lacks reads "missing".
- **Suggested**: the proposed value and where it comes from, with its confidence.
- **Decided**: a value already chosen, and the batch it waits in.
- The rule's instruction, and **Why it matters**, with what goes wrong in SAP.

At the foot are the assignee, **Add a note for the team** with **Add comment**, **History** (every status change, assignment and comment, with who and when) and **Fields the checks read**.

sections.heading: Step 4: decide
sections.text:
On each issue, choose one:

- **Accept** the suggested value. It goes into your draft fix batch and the issue becomes **Fix proposed**.
- **Enter value**, type the right value and select **Save value**. **Keep as is** backs out. On a proposed issue the button reads **Change value**.
- **Not an issue** when the record is right as it is, or **Accept risk** when it is wrong but acceptable. Both ask for a reason, which is kept in the record's history, and both need the approve permission.
- **Undo** takes a proposed value back out of your draft. **Withdraw sign-off** reopens a record marked not an issue.

When a record has more than one suggestion, **Accept all N** at the top accepts them together. After each decision the next record comes up by itself.

sections.heading: Step 5: take and release
sections.text: **Take it** assigns the record to you, so colleagues see it is being worked; **Release** hands it back. Switch on **Mine** to see only your records. Taking needs the assign permission.

sections.heading: Bulk actions
sections.text: Tick the box on each record you want, and a bar appears with **Accept suggestions**, **Take them**, **Release**, **Not an issue** (one reason for all of them), **Undo** and **Clear**.

sections.heading: A whole issue at once
sections.text:
Pick an issue in the **Issues** pane. Two buttons appear above its records:

- **Accept N suggested** gives every open record of the issue its suggested value, in your draft batch. Confirm with **Accept them**.
- **Set one value** gives every open record the same value. **Only records where the field is blank** is on by default, so filled values are left alone. Select **Set value**.

Either action covers up to 50,000 records. If a check failed on more than 100,000 records, the run kept the first 100,000; fix those and the next run lists the rest.

sections.heading: The fix sheet round trip
sections.text:
To work offline or share the work with SAP experts:

1. Filter the list, then select **Download fix sheet**. You get an `.xlsx` workbook with a **Fix sheet** tab: one row per record and failing check, with **Object**, **Record**, **Name**, **Check**, **Severity**, **Issue**, **Field**, **Current value** and **Suggested value**, up to 100,000 rows.
2. Fill in **New value**, or a **Decision**: `fix` (take the suggested value), `not an issue` or `accept risk`, each sign-off with a **Reason**. Leave the other columns as they are.
3. Select **Import fix sheet** and choose the file. Meridian reports how many rows it imported and lists the rows it skipped, such as a sign-off without a reason or a record that no longer fails.

Downloading needs the export permission and importing the apply permission. A file holds at most 5,000 decisions and 25 MB.

sections.heading: Keyboard
sections.text: The keys work while you are not typing in a box: `j` and `k` (or the arrow keys) move, `a` accepts the record's suggestions, `t` takes it, `u` undoes, and `Enter` opens the full record.

sections.heading: New since the baseline
sections.text: When a rule starts failing again, Meridian links to Fix work with **New since** and the date of the baseline run. The list then holds only the records that fail in this run and passed in the baseline, so you see what came back and nothing else. Select the chip to remove the filter. Where the link comes from a single newly failing rule, the list is narrowed to that rule as well. The baseline is explained in [Monitoring](/docs?page=monitoring).

sections.heading: Suggested values
sections.text: There is no separate tab of cleaning proposals. A value Meridian proposes belongs to the record it would fix, so it appears on that record's panel and in the **With a suggested value** figure. Select the figure, or switch on **Has a suggestion**, to list only those records. Then accept a suggestion one record at a time, or take a whole issue at once as described above. Accepting needs the apply permission; approving the batch later needs the approve permission. Old links to the Cleaning proposals tab open Records to fix with the suggestion filter already on.

sections.heading: Comments on a record
sections.text: Every record panel has **Comments**. Write a note, such as why a value is right or who you asked, and select **Add comment**. Comments are kept in order, oldest first, with the record's issue. Adding one needs the analyse permission; without it you can read the thread. A record with no issue yet reads "No issue to comment on".

sections.heading: Raise an exception
sections.text: Some records will not be fixed in this run: the value is right for a legal reason, or SAP will be changed later. Select **Raise an exception** in the record panel, choose the **Severity**, write the reason and select **Raise exception**. The record is tracked under **Exceptions** in the [Inbox](/docs?page=inbox) with its own owner and due date. The button appears for people with the analyse permission.

chapters.title: Approvals and export
chapters.summary: Every value decided in Fix work waits in a fix batch until a second person approves it. The approved batch is then exported as a file your team loads into SAP, and the next run checks whether each rec

sections.text:
Every value decided in Fix work waits in a fix batch until a second person approves it. The approved batch is then exported as a file your team loads into SAP, and the next run checks whether each record now passes. This chapter covers that second half of the work: four eyes, export formats, what the next run does, and what happens after a clean-up, which is covered under monitoring.

Batches are approved in one place, **Inbox**, **Approvals**, beside the SAP write-back requests (see [Inbox](/docs?page=inbox)). Data owners land there. The batches and their export live in **Fix work**, on the **Batches and export** tab, which links to the approvals with **Open approvals**.

sections.heading: Four eyes
sections.text:
A batch always needs two people:

- The person who drafted a batch cannot approve it or export it. The panel says "Four-eyes required: a second person must approve this batch before it can be exported."
- In a batch the monitor drafted, the person who accepted its proposals cannot also approve it.

When a steward accepts suggestions or enters values in Fix work, they land in the steward's own draft batch, named "Fixes by" and the steward's name. A data owner, lead or another steward opens that batch and approves it. Approving needs the approve permission; exporting needs the export permission.

sections.heading: What you see
sections.text:
Three figures follow, and each filters the list:

- **Draft batches**: waiting for proposals to be accepted and approved.
- **Waiting for export**: approved, not exported yet.
- **Still failing after export**: exported records that fail again.

Under them are **Search batches** and the status buttons **All**, **Draft**, **Approved** and **Exported**. The table shows each batch with its **Status**, **Items**, **With proposal**, **Auto-approvable**, **Fixed**, **Still failing** and **Created**. Select a row to open the batch in a side panel.

The panel lists who created and approved the batch and when, then:

- **Items**: each record with its **Field**, **Current** and **Proposed** value, the source, the **Confidence**, whether it is **Accepted**, and **Reconciled** (Fixed or Still failing after the next run).
- **Before and after**: each changed field as `TABLE.FIELD` with its old and new value.
- **Exported files**: each file produced, with its format, who exported and approved it, and its fingerprint, so you can check the file you load is the one Meridian produced.
- **History**: every draft, change, acceptance, approval, export and reconciliation, with who and when.

sections.heading: How to approve and export a batch
sections.text:
1. Open the batch: from **Inbox**, **Approvals** to approve it, or from **Fix work**, **Batches and export**. Both open the same panel.
2. Read the items. While the batch is a draft you can change a proposed value: select it, type the new value and press `Enter`.
3. To accept every high-confidence rule proposal at once, select **Accept N high-confidence proposals**.
4. Select **Approve batch**, then **Approve**. Meridian never posts to SAP; approval is Meridian's record that the values are right. **Not now** backs out.
5. Select **Export batch**, choose the **Export format** and select **Export**.

The formats are:

- **Migration Cockpit workbook (xlsx)**
- **Migration Cockpit CSV**
- **Mass change CSV**
- **Migration Cockpit object templates (xlsx)**
- **MM17 / XD99 / XK99 mass maintenance (zip)**
- **MDG change request file (json)**, which asks for a **Change request type**

Items without a proposed value are not exported. In Fix work, the records of an approved batch read **Approved**; once exported they read **Sent to SAP**.

sections.heading: Loading into SAP
sections.text:
Meridian does not change SAP on its own. Your team loads the exported file through its own controlled process, such as the Migration Cockpit or a mass change transaction. The panel then reads "Exported. Load it with the Migration Cockpit or a mass-change template."

Live write-back is a separate, optional route that is off unless your administrator turns it on. Its requests wait under **Inbox**, **Approvals**, where someone other than the requester approves each one.

sections.heading: What happens on the next run
sections.text:
The next run of the same system, or the next import of the same objects, checks every exported record again. Only runs that finish after the export count.

- A record that now passes becomes **Fixed** in Fix work, and its batch item reads **Fixed**.
- A record that still fails goes back to **To fix**. Its record panel warns: "This value was sent to SAP, but the latest run still finds the record failing. Check the load, or propose another value." The batch item reads **Still failing**, and the figure **Still failing after export** counts it.
- Until such a run, the item shows a dash.

Once a run has finished since the export, **Before vs after** on the batch opens the comparison of the latest run with the run the batch was cut from.

sections.heading: Monitoring after a clean-up
sections.text: After a clean-up, pin the run that shows the cleaned data as the baseline, with **Pin this run as baseline** on the object page. Later runs of that object are then compared with it: the object page shows the rules that started failing again and the records that came back, and when a critical or high rule regresses, Meridian drafts the returned records into a fix batch for you and sends a **Regression** notification. Re-checking, schedules and freshness are explained in [Monitoring](/docs?page=monitoring).

sections.heading: Duplicates
sections.text: Duplicate pairs are reviewed in one place, **Master data**, **Match review**: pairs from the match rules and from the cleaning engine side by side, with **Merge**, **Not a match** and **Skip**. Old links to Fix work's Duplicates tab open it. Merging needs the approve permission. To tune how pairs are found, see [Master data](/docs?page=mdm).

sections.text:
An object is one area of SAP data Meridian scores as a whole, such as Business partner, Material master or an FI general ledger. The Objects pages show which objects are ready, what holds each one back, and every record that fails. Stewards use them to work one object at a time; leads use them to see readiness.

Open **Objects** with its pill in the index bar.

sections.heading: The objects list
sections.text:
The header reads **Objects**, followed by what the list belongs to. With **Latest run** chosen in the scope bar, the list is the current state: each object at the newest finished run of its own system or upload, for example "Current state of 12 objects, latest run 16 Oct 2026". With an older run chosen, it is that run's objects, and the header names the run.

At the top is the object map: one tile per object, sized by records affected, coloured by verdict, with the score on it. Under it are the figures **Go**, **At risk** and **No-go** (select one to filter the list), **Failing rules** and **Critical and high failing rules**. Filter chips for **View**, **Freshness**, **Readiness**, **Dimension** and **Owner** narrow the map and the table together.

The table lists each object with:

- **Blocking rule**: the rule holding the object back, with its description.
- **Records**: records affected.
- **To fix**, **Critical**, **With a suggestion** and **Overdue**: the object's open work from the run's work list. Each number opens the object's records to fix with that filter.
- **Score** and **Verdict**: the score on its ruler, and Go, At risk or No-go.
- **Freshness**: a pill that says whether the object has been checked as often as its cadence promises. See [Monitoring](/docs?page=monitoring).

Choose **Monitoring** under **View** (or open `/objects?view=monitoring`) to swap the work columns for **Checked**, **Cadence**, **Freshness** and **Change** beside the score and verdict. **Change** is the number of newly failing rules since the baseline, with the records in a tooltip. Use the **Freshness** chips to list only the stale, failed or manual objects.

Select a row, or **Open**, to open the object on its **Records to fix** tab, worst record first. The export menu offers the objects as Excel and the analysis report as PDF.

sections.heading: The object page
sections.text:
The header shows the object's name, its score and verdict, the run it belongs to, the failing checks and records affected, the **Owner** and **Steward** pickers and the export menu. A line under it reads "Records of" the object "that fail a check in this run, worst first. Pick one and fix it."

Under it sits the object's monitor, a row of tiles: **Checked**, **Cadence**, **Next check**, **Freshness**, **Baseline** and what changed since the baseline. **Re-check now** starts a new check of the object, and **Pin this run as baseline** makes this run the reference for later comparisons. The tiles are explained in [Monitoring](/docs?page=monitoring).

If anything about this object needs a person, a **To do** card follows, with the item and its button; it is absent when nothing waits. See [To do](/docs?page=todo).

A strip of figures then counts the object's work: **Records to fix**, **Critical records**, **With a suggested value** and **Overdue records**. Each opens the records to fix with that filter. On the **Records to fix** tab the queue's own tiles say the same, so the strip steps aside.

The tabs are **Records to fix**, **Overview**, **Rules**, **Fields**, **Records by rule**, then **Related**, **History** and **Audit**. Press `1` to `5` to jump between the first five.

sections.heading: Records to fix
sections.text:
Every object opens here. It is the object's own slice of [Fix work](/docs?page=fix): the same records, statuses and record panel, for this object only.

1. Narrow the list with **Search by name or key**, the **Issue** list (**All issues**, or one rule with its open count), the **Severity** chips, **Status**, and the **Show** chips **Assigned to me**, **Has a suggestion** and **Overdue**.
2. Pick a record. Each row shows its name or key, its status, the main problem and "and N more issues", the field, its suggestions, an overdue pill and the assignee.
3. Decide in the record panel: accept the suggestion, enter a value, mark it not an issue or accept the risk, take it or release it. The decisions go into your draft fix batch, as in Fix work.
4. Press `j` and `k` to move between records, and `Enter` to open the full record. **Load more** shows the next records.

When every record passes, the tab reads **Every record passes**. If the run's work list is not built yet, a notice offers to build it; see [Troubleshooting](/docs?page=troubleshooting).

sections.heading: Overview, Rules and Fields
sections.text:
- **Overview** starts with **Processes this object feeds**: one tile for each business process that reads this object's fields, such as Procure to pay or Order to cash, with its verdict and how many steps this run blocks. Select a tile to open that process's data readiness for this object and run. Under it are the figures **Failing rules**, **Critical and high failing rules**, **Rule failures** and **Auto-fixable**, the list of failing rules ranked by impact, and the **Score by dimension**. Select a failing rule to read its failing records with the grain it judges at.
- **Rules** lists every rule that ran for the object, with its severity, dimension and records failing. Filter by **Severity**, **Dimension** or **Critical and high**. Select a rule to open its page, with the records, the root cause and the context of the finding.
- **Fields** profiles each table's fields: how often they are filled, their distinct values, and whether a field is masked.
- **Records by rule** lists the failing records of one rule, chosen on the Rules tab.
- **History** draws the object's score over time from the second scored run.

sections.heading: The full record
sections.text: **Full record** in the record panel, or `Enter` in a list, opens the record's own page at `/objects/<object>/records/<key>`. It shows whether the record passes or fails, its identity fields, every failing rule, every field it holds, and, for materials, how complete each view is and any possible duplicates. The record panel sits on the page too, so you can decide here as well. The export menu offers the record's **Fix sheet (PDF)**.

sections.heading: How to assign an owner
sections.text:
1. In the header, choose a person under **Owner**.
2. Choose a person under **Steward**. **Not set** clears either one.

Owners appear in the **Owners** view of Insights, under **More**, **Analysis**, and receive their own digest.

chapters.title: Monitoring
chapters.summary: Meridian keeps watching your data between the times someone opens it. Each object has a cadence, a freshness, a baseline it is compared with and a record of what changed since. This chapter explains w

sections.text: Meridian keeps watching your data between the times someone opens it. Each object has a cadence, a freshness, a baseline it is compared with and a record of what changed since. This chapter explains what those words mean, where to read them and how to change them.

sections.heading: What is monitored
sections.text:
Monitoring is per object. An object is one kind of SAP data, such as Business partner or Material master, read from one system. Every object that has been checked at least once has a monitor, and an object with two checks is already compared with something: you do not have to set anything up first.

You can read the monitor in three places:

- On the object page, a row of tiles sits under the page header.
- On the [Objects](/objects?view=monitoring) list, the **Monitoring** view swaps the work columns for **Checked**, **Cadence**, **Freshness** and **Change** beside the score and verdict. The default view keeps its usual columns and adds **Freshness**.
- On the [To do](/attention) list, an object that has gone stale, a schedule that failed or a rule that started failing becomes an item with its own action.

sections.heading: The tiles on an object page
sections.text:
- **Checked**: how long ago the object was last checked, and what started it: the schedule, an upload, a person's re-check or a person starting it by hand. Select it to open that run. An object that has never run reads **Not checked yet**.
- **Cadence**: how often the object is checked, such as **Daily at 02:00**, **Weekly, Monday 02:00**, **Hourly**, **Manual only** or **Paused**. Times are shown in your organisation's time zone, which an administrator sets under Triage.
- **Next check**: when the schedule will start the next check, or a dash when there is no schedule or it is paused.
- **Freshness**: one pill that says whether the data is as recent as its cadence promises. The next section explains the six states.
- **Baseline**: the run the latest check is compared with. It reads **Pinned run of** a date when someone pinned one, or **Previous run** when Meridian picked the run before it.
- **Newly failing rules** and **Recovered rules**: how many rules fail now that did not fail in the baseline, and how many failed in the baseline and no longer do. The hint under each counts records: select the new failing records to open them in Fix work, or the recovered records to open the comparison of the two runs. Up to two of the newly failing rule IDs are named.

Until an object has a second run, the last tile reads **First run** and says changes show from the second run.

sections.heading: Freshness states
sections.text:
Freshness is judged against the object's own cadence, never against a fixed number of days.

- **Fresh**: green. The last check is on schedule.
- **Due**: neutral. The next check is due now and has not started yet.
- **Stale**: amber. The last check is older than one and a half times the cadence, and never less than two hours, so an hourly schedule that misses one slot is not yet stale.
- **Failed**: red. The last extraction from the system failed. This wins over stale, because the failure is the reason.
- **Paused**: neutral. Someone paused the schedule. A pause is a decision, so it is never stale and raises no to do item.
- **Manual**: neutral. The object has no schedule, for example because you upload files. It shows only how long ago it was checked and is never called stale.

sections.heading: Baseline and drift
sections.text:
The baseline is the reference for "what changed". Two kinds exist:

- A **pinned** baseline is one a person chose, usually the run that shows the data after a clean-up. Select **Pin this run as baseline** on the object page, or **Pin as baseline** on a run. Pinning needs the analyse permission.
- An **automatic** baseline is the previous finished run of the same object. It is used only when nothing is pinned.

Drift is the difference between the latest run and the baseline. **Newly failing rules** is the number to watch. When a rule that matters, one of critical or high severity, starts failing again, Meridian sends a **Regression** notification and puts an item on the To do list. A pinned baseline also lets Meridian draft a fix batch for the records that came back; an automatic baseline never drafts one, because nobody said the data had been cleaned.

sections.heading: Re-check now
sections.text: **Re-check now** on the object page starts a fresh extraction and analysis of that object from its system. It needs permission to trigger syncs on that system; without it the button is visible but asks you to request access. If the object came from an uploaded file there is no system to read, so the button becomes **Upload a new file**. If the object is already being checked, Meridian says so and starts nothing.

sections.heading: Schedules
sections.text:
A schedule tells Meridian to check an object by itself.

- **Set schedule** (when there is none) and **Change schedule** open the system's schedules. Choose a preset or write your own timetable in the standard five-field form. People with permission to manage systems can pause, resume or delete a schedule.
- Open a system, then **Schedules**, to see every object it checks: its cadence, mode (**Full extraction** or **Changes only**), last run, next run and freshness.
- Under the same tab, **Process discovery** lists the business processes that are mined again on a timetable. Select **Add schedule**, choose the process and a cadence. The process page then shows its own **Checked**, **Cadence**, **Freshness** and **Fitness change** tiles. Fitness change is how many points the share of cases that follow the expected flow moved since the run before; a drop of five points or more becomes a to do item.

A run records who started it. On [Runs](/runs), the **Started by** column reads **Schedule**, a person's name, **Upload** or **Re-check**.

sections.heading: When a check fails or is late
sections.text: If a scheduled check fails, the object turns **Failed** and the To do list offers **Retry**. If a schedule misses its slot by more than fifteen minutes, it appears as a missed schedule with **Open schedules**. If an object goes stale, the action is **Re-check now**. Each of these needs the permission to trigger syncs, so only people who can act on them see them. See [To do](/docs?page=todo) for how the list is ranked.

chapters.title: Progress
chapters.summary: Progress answers two questions: how fast is the data getting fixed, and what is slowing it down? Leads use it to report on the clean-up and to see where to put people; stewards use it to see their own

sections.text:
Progress answers two questions: how fast is the data getting fixed, and what is slowing it down? Leads use it to report on the clean-up and to see where to put people; stewards use it to see their own pace. Every number on the page is counted from what the work already records, the record issues, decisions and fix batches, with fixed rules and no model.

Open it with the **Progress** pill. The view has three tabs: **Progress**, **Trends** and **Forecast**. This chapter covers the first; Trends and Forecast are in [Analysis](/docs?page=analysis). The page follows the run chosen in the scope bar. Days are counted as calendar days in UTC.

sections.heading: The figures at the top
sections.text:
- **Open records** (or **Open issues** before the run's work list is built): the records in the run that are still open, that is **To fix**, **Fix proposed**, **Approved** or **Sent to SAP**. The hint gives the number of open issues behind them. Select it to open Fix work.
- **Fixed this week**: issues a run showed fixed in the last 7 days. Only a run can mark an issue fixed; a value waiting for approval does not count.
- **Median time to fix**: the typical number of days from the day a run first found an issue to the day a run showed it fixed, over the fixes of the last 180 days.
- **Projected finish**: the day the open count reaches zero at the recent pace. The pace is the net number of issues closed per day over the last 28 days: the open count 28 days ago minus the open count today, divided by 28. When the pace is zero or negative there is no date, and the figure reads **No date yet**. With nothing open it reads **Done**.

Under the figures are the four sentences: what is open now, what changed in the last 7 days, which object takes longest to fix, and when the backlog clears, with **Open fix list**.

sections.heading: Burn-down
sections.text:
A line of open issues per day over the last 90 days. An issue opens on the day a run first finds it and again whenever it fails after a fix or a sign-off is withdrawn. It closes when a run shows it fixed or someone signs it off. When there is a finish date, a **Projected** line continues at the recent pace, up to 90 days ahead.

Under the line, a bar per run shows the failing record checks in each run of the same system, so you can see each run's step down.

sections.heading: Decisions by person
sections.text: The decisions each person made in the last 30 days, by kind: **Accepted suggestion**, **Typed a value**, **Not an issue**, **Risk accepted** and **Approved**. A bar chart shows the twelve busiest people. **Open work per person** lists each assignee, and **Nobody yet** for unassigned work, with their **Open**, **Critical** and **Overdue** records.

sections.heading: Time to fix
sections.text: For each object, the typical days from first seen to fixed, slowest first. A table per rule shows **Fixed**, **Typical time** (the median) and **9 in 10 within** (the 90th percentile): nine out of ten fixes took that long or less. Only issues a run showed fixed count, over the last 180 days.

sections.heading: Problems that come back
sections.text: Issues that failed again after they were fixed. Each rule and each system shows **Came back**, **Tracked** (issues it has tracked) and **Rate**, the share that came back. A high rate usually means the cause is upstream: a process or an interface keeps writing the bad value, and fixing records alone will not hold.

sections.heading: Where the failing records sit
sections.text: The run's failing records split by the organisational unit in their record key: company code, plant, sales organisation, purchasing organisation or storage location. Use **Slice by** to switch. A Pareto chart shows how few units carry most of the failures, and the table lists **Failing records**, **Still to fix**, **Critical** and **Share of run** for the top 20 values. This tells you which site or company code to talk to.

sections.heading: How good the proposals are
sections.text: For each place a value came from (**Rule suggestion**, **Steward's own value**, **Cleaning engine**, **What-if simulation** or **Entered by hand**): how many values were **Proposed**, how many were **Approved**, **Sent to SAP**, and then **Fixed** or **Still failing** at the next run. **Fix rate** is the fixed values as a share of those the next run could check: fixed divided by fixed plus still failing. A low fix rate on rule suggestions is worth raising with whoever maintains the rules.

sections.heading: Change since the previous run
sections.text: For each object, comparing the run with the run before it from the same system: **New** failing records, **Fixed**, **Still failing**, and **Rules not in both runs**. Only rules that ran in both runs are compared, so a rule added or switched off never reads as a fix. **Open** opens the object.

sections.heading: How to export
sections.text: **Export** offers **Proof of progress (PDF)**, the comparison report for the run, and **Comparison workbook (Excel)**. Exporting needs the export permission.

sections.heading: Team
sections.text: The last section is about the cleaning team, not one run, so it reads live figures. **In progress** is the cleaning items open now, **Within agreed time (SLA)** the share handled in time, and **Capacity** says whether you have enough stewards for the queue: a balance, a surplus or "N stewards short", with how many you have and how many the queue needs. Under them sit the queue's average age and its automation, rejection and rollback rates. **Queue age by stage** shows where items wait longest, **Steward work against the SLA** the last eight weeks of issues and tasks resolved in time, with the open backlog per owner (the policies are under **Triage** in the admin pages), **Bottlenecks** what would clear each waiting stage, and **Sprint plans** suggested batches of fixes with their effect on the score. The old Operations page now opens here.

sections.heading: Good to know
sections.text:
- "Nothing to track yet" means no finished run has found failing records.
- "No earlier run of this system to compare with" means the change card fills after the next run.
- A card that fails to load shows its own error and **Retry**; the rest of the page still works.
